speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a group of experts, I suppose one could call them, is now in the process of distilling the volumes of information that led to the decision. Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to complete the remarks which I started on a previous occasion when this bill was before the House. I would like to set forth some of the considerations and concerns that exist, certainly in my constituency and in the prairie region, regarding railroad conditions, particularly in relation to the CNR. as the condition of the roadbed over which they have to handle trains, often at the risk of their own safety. All of us, no matter what our occupation in life, take a certain amount of risk, but it has become accepted practice in modern times that the risk in all gainful occupations should be minimized. Even in self-employed occupations such as farming, we find the safety councils of the provinces advising farmers to take certain precautions to avoid being injured.
Concern is even expressed about the use of safety belts in privately owned and operated automobiles, as well as about the manner in which the automobile is operated. Concern is expressed about the number of deaths on our highways. In industrial occupations, there is even greater concern regarding the safety of the employees who operate the machines which keep our industrial society going. I have received letters from the brotherhood, and from the workers in my constituency, in which they complain rather bitterly about the conditions to which they are subjected when they work on branch line trains in Saskatchewan. I have put those complaints before the Committee on Transport, as well as before the Transport Commission, and have documented them. It surprised me a little when, with regard to certain derailments on some of the branch lines, the charge was made that the trains were travelling above the speed limit which had been imposed on those tracks. I asked where the report was of the official investigation which had been made which indicated that was the case. If you are going to lay the cause of a derailment or any type of train accident at the door of some individual or group of individuals, the proof should be obtained before the charge is made. I have not seen it yet.
I have here a report from the Railway Transport Committee of the Canadian Transport Commission, dealing with its investigation into three specific accidents. Among the duties imposed upon the Railway Transport Committee by the Railway Act and the National Transportation Act is the obligation of ensuring that all railway operations in Canada are carried out in maximum safety. According to the information which I have,'Mr. Speaker, I do not think this obligation is being carried out. Indeed, I have here a statement made by the railway, as the result of an investigation carried out by an investigator of the Railway Transport Committee, in which it is admitted that the railbed is in poor and unsatisfactory condition.
In addition, I have here a statement made by the local Chairman of the Brotherhood of Enginemen in Biggar in which he states that, in his opinion, three railway subdivisions running out of that town are in such poor condition that safe train operation can not be carried out, and that their condition is a hazard to employees. This is a very serious charge.
Again, quoting from a letter signed by C. W. Rump, Secretary of the Railway Transport Committee, referring to these same divisions, I read:

I question the second part of that sentence in view of the first part which indicates that the three subdivisons are not being maintained to a very high standard. The letter went on to say:
The present level of maintenance work being done on the subdivisions, is not, in our engineer's opinion, sufficient to maintain present conditions; however, as track conditions continue to deteriorate, the railways should further reduce speeds.
Further on in the letter, he said that it had been pointed out to the representative of the railroad that in some cases trains had exceeded authorized speeds.
The point I wish to make again is that to my knowledge no in-depth investigation has been carried out which would entitle anyone to lay the blame at the door of those people who operate the trains. I think there should be an in-depth investigation. I do not think workmen should be required to operate trains under conditions and in circumstances that we know endanger their safety.
As I said when I started to speak, Mr. Speaker, there are times when all of us carry out undertakings that are hazardous, such as getting in a car and driving out of Ottawa on a winter's day when the roads are icy. We know the roads are icy and hazardous, but we choose to run the risk. But I question very much whether as a society we have a right to- ask a crew of men to take out a train, which has a thrust of thousands of tons, under conditions which are known to be hazardous, which the Transport Committee knows are hazardous, and which the railroad, which is owned by the people of this country, is aware are hazardous. I do not see how we can justify that. These are matters that must be given consideration.
As well as that, there is the problem of moving goods over those branch lines. But even this is secondary to the safety of the men who operate the trains. To put it brutally, Mr. Speaker, if a man is injured the cost is too much. And, as shown in this report of the inquiry into three accidents in which one man was killed, we run the risk of killing men. When a man is killed, he is a long time dead. It is a pretty final act. So, I say that the ability to move goods surely must be secondary to the safety of the individuals who are responsible for operating the trains.
When it comes to the question of moving our wheat whether by the CNR or CPR, and in this case we are dealing with the CNR, we must look at the total movement from that little branch line on the Dodsland subdivision right through to Thunder Bay, or Vancouver or Prince Rupert.

speechtext:
I think it is very kind of my friends to enliven proceedings. I am probably making a very dull speech; I would not be surprised if that were the case.
We have to look at the total picture of what is involved, Mr. Speaker. I think that the CNR and the government are suffering from an attitude toward rail transportation that had its origins in the MacPherson commission. The report of that commission was essentially negative. It recommended a cutback in rail transportation suggesting that the railroads be given an amount of money while phasing out parts of their operation in order to rationalize the whole system. Since then, we have been rationalizing so effectively that the safety of the men who work on the railroads is in jeopardy. We have rationalized to the extent that we cannot move a crop of grain from the prairies to the tidewater where ships are waiting. We have rationalized so well that Ontario complains it cannot get lumber from British Columbia and we have rationalized so well that the people of Newfoundland claim their transportation system is chaotic. That has been the effect of rationalization in the past, and now there is a proposal before us for more money so that the system can be rationalized even more. I think the government has a nerve to ask this House for more money without presenting a plan to develop a transportation system which will serve the country.
In reply to a question asked from this side of the House today, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) said that he had met with the representatives of the CNR and they were going to provide some more cars and locomotives. I believe they were to be leased from the United States. He said that he was also to meet with the CPR and that he hoped they were going to do the same thing. Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Transport or the government has to approach our railway companies periodically to ask them if they are going to provide enough equipment to do a job, it indicates how badly our transportation system is organized. Time is lost when it is necessary for the minister or the grain companies or the Canadian Wheat Board to go to the CPR and CNR in order to get action. In the meantime 21 or 22 ships are sitting in English Bay waiting to load and the opportunity for effective action is lost.
What we need without further delay, Mr. Speaker, is an effective program for communication and transportation. A study of grain transportation and handling has been submitted to the Minister in charge of the Wheat Board, but apparently he is afraid to make it public. I suspect it says that if some more branch lines and grain elevators on the prairies were knocked out that would effectively assist in the further deterioration of the facilities and so the whole thing would work better! I suspect there was no consideration at all given to the whole package, and that it will be a long time before this study will see the light of day. This matter requires consideration and the government and the ministers involved should look at the total picture instead of picking out pieces here and there to be patched up when they can no longer be ignored.
When the estimates were before the Standing Committee on Agriculture I asked what research had been done into the facilities for the transportation of grain. The answer was, none. I feel that we could usefully examine in depth the type of carriers and so on that are available. There should be an objective study of the needs of the
CNR and Air Canada
country, and how rail transportation fits in with highway transportation. Storage and handling facilities should also be examined. For example, how can we get a balanced handling at Prince Rupert in relation to the rail and port facilities and the storage available. The same question arises at Churchill. The question of the movement and storage of grain in relation to ice conditions and getting it out to the Atlantic coast should also be examined. In that way we shall obtain a total package, total understanding and real co-operation.
The people who actually operate these trains will have confidence in this system, as will those who use this service, whether they are farmers or lumbermen, to move their products to market. They will be confident that the job will be well done and that the resources of Canada will be available for getting that job done. That is the kind of approach we need. If we adopt that kind of approach, we will have a far better transport system. We will probably need to spend money and put people to work, if the system is to be improved. Yet, why not do that, Mr. Speaker? Would it not be better to put people to work in the areas where they are needed than tolerate a 6 per cent unemployment level and not do those jobs which need to be done? I urge the government to give consideration to an over-all approach to this problem and to say to the CNR, as well as the CPR, "Bring forward a program which will meet the needs of Canadians in Canada." On the day that is done, we shall be able to act effectively in the area of transportation.

Mr. Speaker, I do not imagine anybody pays too much attention to what is said about Bill C-4. However, under our parliamentary system I can still reserve the right to try to make an impression by directing attention to problems that are evident in my part of Canada. I am talking about problems that should be the concern of the government which has a responsibility to provide rail, air and water transportation and associated services, including telecommunications services. I have looked through Hansard to see what has been said about this bill. In my perusal, it has become evident to me that no one, as yet, has mentioned the recommendation accompanying this bill. I therefore feel that it might be worth while mentioning what is contained in the recommendation.
It is recommended by the Governor General to the House of Commons that authorization be given to the CNR to make capital expenditures including investment securities of affiliated companies, in the calendar year 1971, not exceeding $220 million; to make capital expenditures in the first six months of 1972 of some $83 million for discharging obligations incurred prior to January 1, 1972; to further enter into contracts prior to July, 1972, for equipment, additions and conversions requiring payments not exceeding $162 million. It is further recommended that authorization be given to borrow an amount not exceeding $27 million for the construction of branch lines-this is a joke; to make loans and guarantee issues of securities of Air Canada in the amount of $114 million, and even to guarantee debentures in English currency. Without going into too many details, let me say we are

April 21, 1972
CNR and Air Canada
even extending the limits to the magic figure of $1 billion, which probably puts this agency into a special category so far as government expenditures are concerned.
However, the most important part of the recommendation is the part which recommends that this parliament give carte blanche authority for meeting deficiencies in operating revenue, regardless of cost. This is where the hypocrisy lies in all the operations of the Canadian Matronal Railways company. This parliament is expected to give that company permission to write its own cheques up to the sum of $1 billion and we, as protectors of the public money, have no control over that spending. Not only are we to give the company unlimited amounts of money, but this government does not seem to have any control over how the company operates. I wonder if anyone has ever looked carefully at the CN annual report and seen the two pages listing the executives of CNR. On page 30, anyone who wants to look will see listed no less than 30 vice-presidents and assistant vice-presidents as well as another 50 general managers, directors and executive assistants. Mr. Speaker, do you know that all I have ever heard from any of them in my limited dealings with them have been tales of woe as to which railway line they were going to close down or how many employees they were going to lay off or how many stations they would have to close.
I do not know why we complain about the poor Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and all the staff he is gathering around him to try to run the country. I think that all he is trying to do is keep up with the CNR. I have not bothered looking at the executive staff of Air Canada. Frankly, I would hate to look, because I am sure that company must be equally overloaded with executive staff who are quickly learning the way to downgrade service, because they cannot manage a business which has a clearcut monopoly.

speechtext:
At any rate, I hope they do not mechanize their executive staff, because we could expect a big run on manpower offices and we would experience a bigger unemployment crisis than we have now.
Many of my colleagues have expressed themselves quite forcibly on the continuing trend towards the closing down of railway lines which started back in 1968 in Newfoundland. This operation ought to go down in history as the most calculated railroading job that Canada will ever experience. These rail line abandonments have to be about the most ridiculous piece of action you will ever see since, for no reason that sane people can think of, the supposedly responsible authorities stripped my province of the fundamental, basic mode of transport which any country or province must have if it is to build an economy. Without regard for the people who were served by the Newfoundland passenger service and who continue to experience the discomfort and danger inherent in the new method of transportation, these supposedly responsible Canadians, saddled with the responsibility of acting in the best interests of the people, pulled off an act that ought to bother their consciences for the rest of their lives.
I am sure all hon. members will recall the plea that my Newfoundland colleagues made in this House in 1968 when we were stripped of our main transportation ser-
vice. Hon. members criticised us for making our plea and for continuing to make it. What do they think now, those people who are now losing their rail passenger services in the same way as we lost ours? What do those people now think, when the web is closing in on every province of Canada? What did we get in Newfoundland in place of that rail service, Mr. Speaker? We got a bus service. Yes, we got a bus service that was introduced on the basis of a designed strategy and it was introduced before anyone realized the implications of this strategy. The bus service was established without the least bit of consideration of human needs and with no appreciation of the purpose it would serve. That is how the service was established in the province. The service does not suit the climatic conditions of the province and does not fill the needs of the people it was supposed to serve.
Notwithstanding all the expertise that the CN people professed to have, and I mentioned this earlier, it became obvious they did not have a clue as to how to run a bus system, because they started the service without even a basic shelter or station for passengers awaiting the arrival of a bus on the Trans-Canada Highway. People have so stand on the highway in the middle of winter waiting for a bus which is often hours late. There was absolutely no provision for the carrying of invalids who have to travel hundreds of miles sitting up in the bus, or for the carrying of stretcher cases. There was no provision for passengers who had to stand for miles with children in their arms because they could not reserve space in advance or because they lost their seats at station stops when they got off for a bite to eat. Mr. Speaker, there was no planning whatsoever; and then the CNR bragged about their cheap prices and oversold tickets. Now, the company is applying to the appropriate provincial agency for a 30 per cent increase in bus fares. Let me tell you that some passengers had to hire taxis to follow the bus. There have been cases where people had to get to the hospital, and they hired a taxi to follow a bus in the hope that a passenger would get off at a stop and make a seat available.
Let me tell you about one of the communities served by this Canadian dream bus system in my district of Newfoundland. There is at the community of Howley, which is some 30 miles from Deer Lake, a station stop for buses. Anyone travelling from Grand Falls to Howley has to go 30 miles beyond Howley to Deer Lake because the bus will not stop at the junction, and then hire a taxi to travel that same 30 miles back home. That is the system presently set up. About three years ago when the president of CNR appeared before a committee, I asked him if the company had had any experience with providing bus services. He said they had not had such experience. I then asked why the company had not approached a bus company like Greyhound, or some similar company, for advice on how to set up a bus service. Now, after an interval of four years, CNR is going to Greyhound and asking that company to tell them what is wrong with the bus service presently provided in Newfoundland.
This is the system they set up. These expert executives are listed in the CN report as corporate planners, as vice-presidents of express and highway services, as marketing specialists, as experts in passenger sales and ser-
April 21, 1972

vice and as experts in research and development. These are the people who planned and provided this bus system which should be the laughing stock of Canada. I could tell you about the people living in small communities which are away from the main highway. These people have to hire taxis to get to the bus because the CNR does not provide a feeder service. This same company, the CNR, keeps feeding monthly figures through the press about all the passengers they carry and the increase in the passenger load. What else can one expect when there is no other way to travel. They give a service alright, so long as people live on the trans-Canada highway.
Let me tell you what else they are doing in Newfoundland for the Canadian dream. For years, private individuals have provided a bus service under provincial licence by the Board of Commissioners of Public Utilities, an arm of the provincial government. This commission is almost a part of the Jessie James bargain, imposed when the agreement was made to eliminate the rail passenger service. These private bus companies provided a service under the worst road conditions before the advent of the trans-Canada highway. They eked out a bare living. Now, what has happened? As soon as the CN was ready, it obliterated the small businessmen. It will continue to do so as road conditions improve. It will not serve communities which are not on paved highways. However, as soon as the roads leading to these communities are paved, the CN will move in and put the small operator out of business. We talk about unfair competition under the Competition Act. I hope the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andras) will look into this matter. Every small bus operator will be out of business in the next few years as the octopus CNR closes its tentacles around the rest of the province. We in Newfoundland demand the return of our railway service because it is vital to our economy. We demand the return of the railway system because its continuance was guaranteed under the terms of confederation. There is no reason this cannot be done, because all that is required is improvement of the rails, the cutting out of some of the curves, which should have been done in years past.
Although I doubt it, I hope that someone will listen and this will come about. We demand a rail passenger service because of the repeated promises by this government that every Canadian will be accorded equality of opportunity, regardless of where he lives. We demand it because of the stated objective of the Canadian Transport Commission just last year, the development of a basic transcontinental passenger service which will justify whatever cost there may be to the federal treasury and which will satisfy the needs of the travelling public. This has to be done for all Canadians from coast to coast. If the commission cannot fulfil this promise they should resign, and the government should resort to its usual procrastinating task force concept to find out why the rail service is not being provided. It may not be too long before they will no longer have any control over it. Probably, however, I am being a little too insular in my attitude towards the Canadian transportation scene as a whole. We have all become aware that the automobile is one of the major sources of pollution, as is the supersonic transport in the skies.
CNR and Air Canada
Let us look for a moment at a booklet issued by The United Transportation Union. Under the heading "Does Government Care?" we find this:
But the question remains: Who's going to save the passenger train in Canada? Certainly not the railways. They continue the systematic process of dismantling their passenger services, with the blessing of the federal government and its agency, the CTC.
It is ironic to recall that the CPR once promised that it would "forever efficiently maintain, work and run the Canadian Pacific Railway," in exchange for vast grants of land and cash and generous tax concessions from its friends in government.
Further down on the same page there is this:
If the government were seriously concerned with the kind of transportation services Canadians are getting, it would force the CPR to change its priorities.
Then another part of the booklet reads:
The history of the CNR is evidence enough that nationalization alone is no guarantee of good service. At any rate, the government seems to have no objection at all to the CPR's priorities, and neither does the Canadian Transport Commission, which under the National Transportation Act administers transportation policy.
The Act is largely responsible for the uncertain future of passenger service in this country. Its passage was Jack Pickersgill's crowning achievement as transport minister, and it seems to be deliberately designed to encourage the railways to get rid of their passenger trains. If a railway wishes to abandon a service, it must first prove that it is losing money on it to the satisfaction of the CTC. Then the Commission, after considering "all matters that in its opinion are relevant to the public interest," rules on whether the railway can go ahead with the abandonment. If it says no, the railway must keep it going and the government will subsidize its losses on the service to the extent of 80 per cent.
This provision came into effect just after the rail passenger service in Newfoundland was eliminated. Nobody told the CN they could continue the service and apply for the 80 per cent subsidy. They cut out the service on the assumption that it was costing $900,000 a year. This is ridiculous.
Moving on for a moment to other responsibilities of the CNR, I wish to bring into question again, as I have on other occasions, the ferry service between the Island of Newfoundland and Labrador. St. Barbe North, which is in my district of northern Newfoundland and which everybody seems to forget, is in northern Canada. In spite of all the policies and millions of dollars being poured into northern Canada, and in spite of all the need for the movement of goods and services between Newfoundland and Labrador over a distance of 10 or 15 miles, we cannot seem to get the government to realize the need for a proper wharf so that the ferry can dock and so that the service may operate in a modern way. Many papers come across my desk indicating what the Canadian government intends to do about the north. I must say that it would seem that the northern part of Canada in my riding of northern Newfoundland gets little or nothing. I demand that this ferry service be looked into, and I hope the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) will do so.
There are many weaknesses in Air Canada's service and I hesitate to go into them, but it is obvious that the transportation system, particularly in my province, leaves much to be desired. It is difficult to understand why the government, on the one hand, spends many millions of dollars creating new agencies like Information Canada and, on the other hand, cannot provide a service in the

April 21, 1972
CNR and Air Canada
province of Newfoundland. This seems to be beyond comprehension. I can only ask that the government take another look at the situation or even speak to me, because I am willing to meet with them and discuss the matter. This might allow me to get over my frustration because I feel the province of Newfoundland should be considered as a part of the Canadian dream.

Mr. Speaker, the CNR financing bill before us brings to the attention of hon. members a potpourri of problems relating to transportation across the country.
But there are four main areas of concern-financing, pensions for employees, passenger transportation services in relation both to rail and air transport, and the involvement of the government in future planned development. If two ministers should be here today, they should be the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson). The only official person I see here today, however, is the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Buchanan). Well do I recall his speech when he introduced the legislation on behalf of the government. I believe it lasted for no more than ten minutes, probably for about seven minutes. It was the type of speech one would make to a Kiwanis Club or to a Kinsmen's Club or to a Chamber of Commerce. It was innocuous. It was anaemic. It was a nothing speech. Yet here we are, considering areas of concern which affect all Canadians. One would think the government would make a determined attempt to be persuasive and put forward a convincing defence of the position it has taken.
This has not happened. When I think of the Minister of Transport, I remember the late "Satchmo" Armstrong. "Satchmo" Armstrong was a man who was all smiles. His gravel voice put out a multiplicity of words. What he performed on the trumpet was really sweet music. The Minister of Transport is all smiles and he is all sweet talk. The difference is that he blows nothing on his trumpet. Nothing comes out. He is all puff, but there is no performance. It is a sad note that he is not here today. It is sad to think he has not been here during the debate to listen to the representations made by various members of the House concerning the troubles they have encountered in the field of transportation.
I appreciate that the areas of responsibility which the minister must assume in the railway and transportation fields are wide. But it seems to me, from his performance so far, that he has been a captive of his officials, that he has become the yo-yo of their policies and decisions. Substantially, they have no policies and, in fact, they make very few decisions unless those decisions are dictated to them or influenced by CNR officials.
I notice, now, that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) is presently in the House. I hope he will bring to the attention of his colleague, the Minister of Transport, that he has been compared with "Satchmo" Armstrong. I compare the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce with Maurice Chevalier.

speechtext:
It is unfortunate there is a time limitation, otherwise I could spend the afternoon moving from one minister to the next.
May I say that the Minister of Transport has really contributed nothing new, nothing dynamic, nothing constructive to the solution of the main problems facing us today in the transportation field. Your Honour will recall that I said there were four areas which were of particular concern. The first concerns finance. The CNR has been the recipient of the financial burdens of railways which were operated by private enterprise in the past and which failed. When reorganization took place around 1920, the CNR assumed those responsibilities. From that time until today it has continued to bear this burden in the form of bonds and liability for interest payment. These liabilities have proved to be an albatross around the neck of the CNR and have, indirectly, been the cause of a great deal of unfair criticism directed toward a public enterprise. Critics of public enterprise point a finger at the CNR and say: This is an example of what happens when an enterprise is taken over by the government. They do not go back into history and remember that the CNR was saddled from the beginning with an almost impossible task.
I would imagine that the main question we should be asking ourselves is this: How can we best approach the rationalization of this financial position? How can we set up a financial structure which would give the CNR an opportunity to succeed? I hasten to add that the CNR has shown a profit on its yearly operations in terms of the profit and loss sheet. The difficulty has arisen with regard to the repayment of the bond holders in connection with the debt the railway assumed around 1920. One would
April 21, 1972

think, therefore, that the government would consider taking the initiative by paying past debts of the company and setting up a new financial structure.
It appears to me that the financial problem to which I have referred could repeat itself in the area of air transportation. Air Canada has in the past had the exclusive right to provide air transport, but from the time it was set up to the present day there has been a whittling away of the monopoly that Air Canada should have in the provision of air transport. The CPR entered the air transport field and has taken away some of the routes Air Canada served in the past. We now have other air transport companies entering the field, again trying to fragment and to whittle away the monopoly that Air Canada should have. The small companies, with their so-called feeder services, are attempting to encroach upon the operations of Air Canada. Need I mention the recent application of TransAir, which now wants to provide passenger service from Toronto to Winnipeg, thereby again cutting in on the service of Air Canada.
Surely, the day will be reached when the operations of Air Canada will be so fragmented by the encroachment and intrusion of private air companies that we may find a repetition of what happened to the railway services in 1918, where finally the private companies failed and were merged into the CNR. I suggest you may find Air Canada failing in the future as a result of the intrusion and encroachment of private companies. Then, the logical result would be that the private air companies would fail, and then the business people would look to Air Canada to assume their debts and also to acquire their routes.
One of the things that worries me is that, with the setting up of the Canada Development Corporation, there has been a great deal of talk about such companies as Air Canada and Polymer being purchased by the Canada Development Corporation, then shares being issued which would be made available to the public. I can almost anticipate what would happen, Mr. Speaker. I do not think one has to be an old testament prophet or a Jeanne Dixon, a woman we hear about in the United States who forecasts the future, to see what might happen. We will find the CDC, by assuming the assets and operations of Air Canada and Polymer and making shares available to the public, stressing the profit aspect of their business operations and forgetting the service aspect.
In that situation the corporation would be concentrating on profit rather than on service, and it may get into the same hoary mess that the CNR has got itself into in the field of transportation. I hope that this does not happen. I hope that the parliamentary secretary will take the message back to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) and have him spend a weekend in retreat thinking through some of the problems that have been presented to him by all members of this House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, prior to the luncheon adjournment you will remember that I said there were four main areas of criticism with regard to the performance of this government in the transportation field, both in its railway service and its airport service. You will recall that I said that first, the criticism related to financing, second, to pensions, third, to passenger service, and fourth, to the involvement of the government in land development. I underlined, in my usual low key style, that the performance of both the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) has been very bad, not only so far as their lack of attendance to hear the representations of the different members of the opposition is concerned but also as regards the performance of the officials of the Department of Transport.
With regard to pensions, I said that the government was applying the divide and rule theory to CNR employees so far as their pensions are concerned, according to which the government pays only 11 per cent of the salary of the employee during his years of service and the calculation is based on his best five years of service. The example that I gave was that if an employee worked for 20 years he would receive 11 per cent per year of service which would make 30 per cent of his best five year average salary, whereas the federal civil servants obtain 2 per cent per year under the same formula. Therefore, the federal civil servants receive 40 per cent of their salary while the CNR employees receive 30 per cent which, in my opinion and that of many others, is rank discrimination and unfairness. Not only that, there is also the question of the recent catch-up payment made by the government to meet some of the shortages that railway employees were experiencing in the country. I think the government gave them a one-shot payment to make up the difference, whereas the federal civil servants have a continuing formula. Therefore, again there is discrimination with regard to the railway employees.
This indicates the callous, indifferent and political attitude of this government concerning pensions of CNR employees. This divide and rule theory has been applied not only to CNR employees but to the senior citizens of this country. The government has used the same technique with regard to cost of living payments to people who only recieve old age security payments and to those who receive old age security plus the supplement. The people who receive old age security and who have contributed a great deal to this country are thereby denied any cost of living bonus. This principle is being applied to the CNR employees, and many of us look on it as a double standard used by the government. We think it is distasteful and disdainful.
The third area of criticism that we in the opposition have relates to the passenger service performance of the CNR. Over the years I have heard many people refer to the great performance of Mussolini in Italy who made the trains run on time. I have also heard comments regarding the fantastic railway service in Japan, as well as the fast, efficient and well administered railway service in certain 
European countries. The question arises, why are these tributes paid to these countries but when it comes to the transportation in Canada people are dismayed and disgusted. Some say that it is because of the public ownership principle in countries such as Japan, Italy and other European countries where the public demands efficiency. Here, we have historical facts which run against us, where we have one railway line operated under public ownership and the other, the CPR, under private ownership. This conflict does not produce an efficient type of service which people want and expect.
The tragedy with regard to the railway service is that the CPR dominates the transportation scene in Canada. When they decide, for example, to abandon the passenger service, the government says "yes, sir, we will assist you to do so". So they abandon rail lines and services while the government stands idly by and the minister takes no active part to protect the people of this country. When the CPR says that they will discontinue the passenger service because it brings no profit but they will continue freight service because it brings profit, then it is high time for the government to take the initiative and set down a transportation policy which would meet the needs of all Canadians. Surely, the time has come when the CPR should be confronted with the situation which exists in transportation, and if they have ideas regarding the discontinuing of passenger service then I hope we will not make the same mistake as was made by the CNR back in 1918 when private companies failed and their debts were assumed by the CNR. I hope that if any compensation is given it will be minimal, because what we need across the country is an integrated service which will meet the needs of all Canadians and which will use up-to-date transportation techniques, not only with regard to passengers but with regard to products.
When one reads of track air cushion vehicles and yet find we have had no real research and development by the CNR in this area, one wonders what they have in mind with regard to future development in this field. This also brings to question the cummuter train service which to date has been haphazard and very inefficient. I hope that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Buchanan) will bring to the attention of the Minister of Transport some of the failings that we have experienced in the transportation service.
With regard to our air service, lately we have had the problem of the new airport in Toronto. You will recall that a few years ago when air transport needs were very pressing in Toronto, the government recommended the expanded use of the Toronto international airport at Malton. You will recall also that the hon. member for Peel-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beer), and other hon. members who were directly affected raised such a furore with the government that it backed down and changed its decision with regard to any future expansion of the Malton airport. I notice that the hon. member for Peel-Dufferin-Simcoe is present this afternoon.
I think I should say to him that I am not being unduly critical of him, or the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Chappell) with regard to the opposition from their constituencies concerning expansion of the Malton airport. But what

I am saying is that this would indicate a lack of planning with regard to an expanded airport at Malton. To permit builders to build homes so close to Malton airport, when the government should have had the foresight to know the area would be required for expansion, makes me believe the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) has been negligent in the performance of his duties.

I apologize to the hon. member for not naming his constituency correctly. Mr. Speaker, I was sad to read the news that he is about to retire from his constituency. I hope he enjoys the full benefits of his pension. As 1 was saying, the representations made by the members representing these constituencies were so valid and strong that the government backed down with regard to expanding the Malton airport. As a result we had a continuation of the problem of transport in Toronto.
Then, the government brought forth the second suggestion, that the airport should be located at Pickering, and for the last while we have had discussions with regard to the new location. It would be fair to say that the Liberals are incomplete disarray concerning it. Here I mention the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik). When I think of him. Mr. Speaker, I think of Charlie McCarthy because he appears to be speaking out of both sides of his mouth. He appears to be saying yes to some, and no to others. It will be interesting to see which side he comes down on with regard to the site.
I also think of the hon. member for York North (Mr. Danson) who, when the motion concerning CNR financing came up, did not touch on the airport at Pickering but said he would prefer the new airport to be located at Peterborough. Actually, he indicated he was in favour of the airport at Pickering, but when the flack reached his ears from constituents who found that the flight pattern would be right over their property he had to take the position that many people take when trade unions become involved in organizing. It is known as the mug-rump position. They have their mug on one side of the fence and their rump on the other. He reminds me of the fellow who goes to the old swimming hole, takes off his clothes, goes in for a swim, comes out, finds his clothes missing, and runs around screaming, wondering where they are. The hon. member for York North is running around screaming trying to find out what position he should take.
What do we need with regard to a new airport in Toronto? First of all, Mr. Speaker, we must establish that there is a need for a new airport. Secondly, if there is a need, we must establish what is the best location. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) sent a letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on this matter, and in it touched on two problems that exist. In it he wrote:
First of all, I do not believe that any convincing case has been made out for the need for a new international airport in the Toronto area. If such a need exists it should be shown to the public to exist. Secondly, assuming the need, I do not believe that

a case has been made out for the site now chosen as the best possible site.
Then, he pointed out a precedent in England which most of us should know about. I quote:
I note that in the United Kingdom when in the planning stages of developing a third London airport, a commission of inquiry, the Roskill commission, was created to advise the British government as to its timing and location. The commission engaged a research team and a number of outside consultants. Public hearings were held to establish the facts and a further public hearing was held in London following publication of a cost benefit analysis. The commission made its report and it was submitted to the government.
The public was invited to present its arguments in favour or contrary to the proposed plan. Witnesses were cross-examined to ensure that the strengths and weaknesses of the evidence would be made apparent.
I think this should be the approach with regard to the new site at Pickering. I am not alone in this belief because I notice that the Ontario Liberal leader, Robert Nixon said recently that the province might as well hold public hearings immediately on the proposed Pickering airport. He is attempting to say that the onus is on the Ontario government with regard to public hearings. In light of the new expropriation laws that have been passed, I think the government will take the position that there must be public hearings, and will have them held under the provisions of that act. That is not adequate, because under the Expropriation Act there is no requirement on the person holding a hearing to delve into all the pros and cons. His jurisdiction is too narrow for that.
What we need is a public inquiry along the same lines as they had in England, where a commission was set up which made a detailed study. A report was submitted to the government and then the government submitted that report to a public inquiry to determine the pros and cons. This would be a fine example of participatory democracy. At the moment, we have only the Minister of Transport acting in a very cute and shy, concealing way with regard to the government's plans.
My final point deals with the participation of the government in land development. The example I have in mind is Metro Centre in Toronto, a development of the southern part of the city towards the lake, extending roughly from Yonge Street to Bathurst, and embracing a good number of acres. This venture has required the joint participation of the CNR and the CPR. Very little public information has been given out by the CNR or by the minister with regard to the government's involvement in Metro Centre. I would like the parliamentary secretary, and possibly the officials in the gallery to make note of some of the questions I have received concerning Metro Centre. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I note that you are keeping your eye on the clock. I would like to remind you that we did not start until 12 minutes after two o'clock and so I have another five minutes to go.
These are some of the questions that I have received: one, what happens when a public corporation, the CNR, and a private corporation get together and produce an offspring, namely, Metro Centre Development? Surely, the legitimacy of the results of such a union should be questioned? Two, what has the CNR contributed to this union? How is it being financed? Three, what reason does CNR give for tearing down Union Station and building a new terminal just south of the present Union Station site?

Four, how much land within the Metro Centre area does CNR hold title to, and approximately where is it located? Five, what guarantees can CNR give that in the event a new terminal is built, passengers will not be inconvenienced by longer walking distances between subway, GO-trains and mainland trains?
What guarantee can the Canadian National provide to GO-train passengers that the new terminal will be located no further from the center of the city than the present Union Station? Has the Canadian National investigated the possibility of retaining the present post office terminal 'A' building for an air terminal and, later, bus terminal? Has Air Canada shown any interest in retaining the post office downtown for an air terminal where outgoing passengers can be ticketed and transferred to Malton by rail, thereby bypassing the passenger terminal at Malton? Is the Canadian National engaged in any studies to provide additional commuter passenger train service, in co-operation with the province of Ontario? Is the Canadian National engaged in research, or is it sponsoring research with regard to track air cushion vehicles? Those are some of the questions submitted to me with regard to the Metro Centre, and I hope we get answers to them. As I said at the beginning of my speech, four main areas have been covered but we have had little or no response and the only conclusion must be that the government feels "the public be damned, long live private enterprise". I am ashamed if that is their position.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-4, to finance and guarantee funds to the CNR and Air Canada provides the annual opportunity for members of this House to discuss transportation problems. These two companies service most of Canada, along with the CPR and CPA and so transportation problems in Canada in general may be touched upon as well as any specific cases. The lack of a viable transportation policy affects people from one coast to the other and the economic problems involved concern all members.
In commenting upon this bill this afternoon, I should like to be as objective as possible. I certainly do not intend to mention political parties because this problem affects all of us. However, in Atlantic Canada Transportation has always been a problem and, in fact, the basis of our entry into Confederation was access to the central Canadian markets. In fact, the Maritime Freight Rates Act was supposed to guarantee that Atlantic Canada would have equal access to the central Canadian markets, but regardless of what party was in power, problems have existed.
On March 14, when the minister introduced the bill he outlined the problem. While some of his speech was interesting and philosophic, I felt that he tended to ignore the historic right of equal access given in the Maritime Freight Rates Act. He mentioned that our freight rate increases are under the national average, notwithstanding the fact that we have had eight increases in the past 29 months. I should like to illustrate how these increases affect a manufacturer in my area. Ironically, two years ago this manufacturer received assistance through a DREE grant in order to expand his plant so that he could compete in Canada. His ability to do this is seriously

impaired by these freight rate increases in such a short period.
The Maritime Freight Rates Act was designed to give goods manufactured in the Atlantic provinces access to the central Canadian market. When there is a freight rate increase across the board of, say, 10 per cent, that has less impact on the short-haul shipment from Ottawa to Toronto or Montreal than it has on the long-haul shipment from Halifax to Montreal or Vancouver. This has been recognized by various transportation commissions and they have attempted to resolve it. The formula in the Maritime Freight Rates Act represented an attempt to solve the problem, but now that act has been superseded. It is not good enough for the minister to say that our freight rate increases are still under the national average. Because of the distance involved, any increase hits us harder than it hits the shipper in central Canada.
The MacPherson Royal Commission stated in volume one of its report at page 18 as follows:
It is the regions of Canada where competition to the railways is less intense upon which the present freight rate structure bears most heavily. Although monopoly no longer characterizes the transportation system as a whole in Canada, there are still vestiges of it in areas which, because of inadequate highway facilities, distance from markets, or other factors which have inhibited the development of competition, continue to be dependent to varying degrees on railway transport. While it is true that the number of competitive rates and agreed charges is growing in both the Atlantic provinces and western Canada, the indications are that they are comparable neither in quantity nor quality to those applicable within central Canada.
And here is the important part, Mr. Speaker:
The end result appears to be that the uneven impact of competition, transmitted through the freigh rate structure, tends to produce a greater relative increase in the price of moving goods by rail for the Atlantic and western shipper than that experienced bv shippers in Central Canada. This effect is particularly noticeable on long-haul shipments to the markets of central Canada. For example, the marketing consequences of a 20 per cent increase to a long-haul shipper who has been paying $500 a carload to get his product to the Toronto market and will now pay an additional $100 are obviously more serious than those upon his short-haul competitor who has been paying $50 a carload to get to the same market and will now pay only $10 more.
In Atlantic Canada, there are not too many viable companies manufacturing the basic necessities, but I should like to illustrate the impact of this freight rate increase on a company in my riding, the Canadian Keyes Fibre Company, Limited. As a result of the last freight rate increase, and there have been eight over the last 29 months the last talking place on February 14, 1972, the transportation manager of the company wrote to the minister and pointed out in graphic terms how these freight rate increases, one piled on top of the other, are pushing this company to the brink of survival, since most of its customers are in the west and central parts of Canada. He wrote:
On February 14, industry in Nova Scotia, and across Atlantic Canada will be faced with an increase in most rail rates, ranging from 4-8 per cent. Some people may say "so what, a rate increase of 4-8 per cent in many industries would not be considered unrealistic." The startling thing about this increase is that it is the eighth time in the past 29 months that rail rates have increased!
Canadian Keyes Fibre Company Limited, located in Hantsport, Nova Scotia, manufactures a variety of molded wood pulp prod-
April 21, 1972

ucts such as Egg Cartons, Berry Boxes, trays for packing eggs, meats, produce, etc., Pie Plates for bakeries and disposable tableware. We presently employ approximately 325 people.
Most of our products are made from raw materials produced in Nova Scotia, utilizing the natural wood resources of our Province. These finished goods are sold in all major markets across Canada. We are, therefore, a "resource" industry that makes a major contribution to the real wealth of our Province. A very minor portion of our production is exported outside of Canada.
He went on to say:
We feel sure that if a manufacturer as vital to the economy as rail transportation were to apply increases at the rate of 8 times in 29 months, and a cumulative total of some 35-68 per cent, government action would very likely be considered.
We know, Mr. Speaker, that when the St. Lawrence Seaway workers were given a 30 per cent pay increase over a two-year period, there were objections. Some members in this House as well as people around the country, say that our present inflationary spiral can be traced back to that fantastically large increase, in percentage terms, which was granted to those workers. People have criticized that increase bitterly. As the writer points out, cumulative increases of between 35 and 68 per cent in other areas would bring cries of outrage from the members of this House. He illustrates how these increases have affected the transfer of goods from Hantsport, where the company exists, to the various shipping points where the customers are. I will not read the entire list. It is interesting to note that the rate from Hantsport to Cornerbrook was $1.13 on January 1, and now it is $1.81. From Hantsport to Montreal, the rate on January 1, 1969, was 93 cents; on February 14, after the last increase, it rose to $1.37. I might mention that these are increases on class 45 carload rates to these various points.
The rate to Toronto went up from $1.30, on January 1, 1969, to $1.84, after the last increase. To Winnipeg, the rate was $2.99 in January, 1969, and went up to $4.13 after the last increase in February. To Calgary, the rate went from $4.65 in January to $6.08, and to Vancouver it increased from $5.65 to $7.39. In view of these increases, one wonders how the company can continue competing in the markets of Canada. Instead of philosophizing about the national average of rate structures and saying that perhaps we are not far above or below that national average, the minister should consider how any across the board increase adversely affects the long-haul shipper, be he in the east or in the west.
These increases constitute real discrimination against relatively depressed areas of the economy and make it difficult for companies in those areas to compete. Apparently the minister either does not acknowledge the problem or has underplayed its seriousness. Certainly, the point at issue is not any national average for rate increases. That is not the point at all. The point we must consider is the history behind the maritimes freight rates legislation. That legislation was originally introduced to guarantee our producers access to the markets of central Canada. A subsidy was paid. That is no longer the case under the National Transportation Act. Consequently, the long-haul shipper, whether in the east or in the west, is much harder hit now with across-the-board increases.
I think the traffic manager of the company was most moderate in suggesting to the minister that such action
CNR and Air Canada
should not be taken again without further study, and that the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission ought to be involved in any study before there are any increases. In his letter he spoke about the impact of these freight rate increases and suggested that their impact be assessed before further increases are piled on top of the ones already imposed during the last 29 months. He suggested, further, that the minister obtain a progress report from the federal-provincial committee which was set up to examine the recommendations made by the premiers of the four Atlantic provinces in March, 1969. These actually have not been fully implemented. Only one or two of those recommendations have been implemented, most of the others are gathering dust.
The former minister of transport who is now the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) requested concrete suggestions on how to resolve these fundamental problems. We waited for two years while four Atlantic premiers of different political stripes set up a joint study. Federal funding was involved. In the end, the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Committee made recommendations that were unanimous. They were adopted by the Atlantic premiers, who adopted them regardless of political stripe. For the first time we had a report from the four Atlantic premiers, and it set out clearly positive steps that should be followed if the perennial problem of transportation was to be resolved. Since then, another minister of transport from eastern Canada has been appointed. Certainly, he is aware of these recommendations and is as vitally concerned about them as we are. Unfortunately, the mechanism that the premiers wanted to establish for resolving these problems is not in operation. The federal-provincial committee set up to continue the work begun by the four Atlantic premiers has not followed the recommendations of the four premiers.

As my friend from Moncton has reminded me, the minister ignored the unanimous report of the transport committee that had travelled through Atlantic Canada. Ironically, it was tabled in the House on the very day when the minister brought in the most recent transportation bill, the Atlantic transportation fiscal arrangements act, or something like that, in 1969. We went to all the trouble of travelling around the various areas of Atlantic Canada. I was a member of the committee, as was my good friend from Moncton. This commitee heard all the government groups, the boards of trade, the manufacturers groups and the farm groups. The committee came back here and prepared a unanimous report which was not a political partisan document.
The great irony is that the report was tabled in the House of Commons on the very day the Transport Minister brought in the Atlantic transportation fiscal arrangements bill, as I believe it was called, a piecemeal transportation bill to help solve part of the Atlantic transportation problems. At that time, the minister said that other bills would follow after the transportation committee report was evaluated, and after the Atlantic premiers report was

assessed. That was in 1969, and we still have not had further items dealing specifically with Atlantic transportation. One might leave out the criticism I have made in respect of these eight increases over a period of 29 months and say I am being parochial in talking about Atlantic Canada. Of course I am, because I have the honour to represent a riding in that part of Canada.
Let us leave the question of the lack of Atlantic policies and talk about the general transportation policy in Canada or the lack of one. The National Transportation Act was supposed to be the great blueprint for all time. This is the act which created the Canadian Transport Commission. The Minister of Transport who piloted the bill through this House became the first chairman of the Canadian Transport Commission. I refer of course to Mr. Pickersgill who is now Chairman of the CTC. Even since 1969, there have been so many changes that some of the underlying premises of the National Transportation Act as we have seen it implemented should be challenged. I think the compensatory rates for competitive modes of transport must be seriously considered. I wonder whether they are really valid. As I wonder this, I should like to draw attention to what the Canadian Railway Labour Association thinks about a national transportation policy, or the lack of one. This organization made the following submission to the government on March 6, 1972:
We agree with the general principles of the 'National Transportation Policy' but suggest that it does not go far enough towards meeting the needs of the Canadian public. For example, the national transportation policy should be directed towards the fullest use possible of Canadian transportation facilities in the movement of our natural resources to export positions. We have in mind such cases as the exporting of coal from the Kootenay region of British Columbia to the Roberts Bank superport which was constructed partially with Federal funds. Our contention is that the movement of such Canadian natural resources should be restricted to Canadian modes of transport using Canadian routes. We further contend that such issues should be dealt with on a national level, that there should be a national policy for dealing with these issues, and that they should not be left with a provincial regulatory body or a provincial government. In addition in the application of the policy to date vis-a-vis the rail passenger situation, too much emphasis has been placed on the narrow concept of economic viability.
We have emphasized throughout this Brief the existence of change and the many ways in which change should affect policy in Canada. One dominant reason why change should bring about new and different policies is because, with the passage of time, the assumptions upon which existing policies are based become less valid, if not erroneous.
That is what I say has happened in respect of the National Transportation Act. The brief continues:
A case in point, and one which is of great importance to us is the National Transportation Act. Many of the basic assumptions upon which this Act is based date back to the MacPherson Royal Commission in the 1950s. We are very strongly of the view that many of the conclusions of the studies done for that Royal Commission are not consistent with contemporary views. The Act contains a built-in bias towards using economic viability as the over-riding criterion for determining railway passenger transportation needs. We suggest that the assumptions upon which the Act was based are not a sufficient basis for contemporary policy and that these assumptions are in contradiction with many of the Government's other policies.
The assumptions of the Act are insufficient today because the Canadian people and their Government have increasingly realized that while economic criteria are important, perhaps the most important criteria, they should not be the overriding consideration

in all cases. This is especially true when one considers the longterm results of any given action. We have realized that while the gross national product may be a reasonably satisfactory aggregate measure of the Canadian people's well-being, it is a poor measure of the quality of life.
Increasingly also economics and the other social sciences have placed renewed emphasis upon a vastly broadened concept of cost, realizing that public costs and benefits can, and frequently do, outweigh private costs and benefits. To consider only costs and benefits in a narrow sense is to accept a short-term and unrealistic framework for policy. It is not sufficient for the Canadian Transport Commission to look at the costs and revenues as submitted by the railways for such a service and merely weigh those arguments against the views of the public at a hearing.
This Government has increasingly demonstrated its willingness to view problems on a long-term basis and to do so within the framework of a broadened concept of costs and benefits, especially with respect to environmental questions. But your willingness to be farsighted on some environmental issues contrasts sharply with the underlying assumptions of the National Transportation Act, which is the basic element in Canada's transportation policy.
There are numerous ways in which the National Transportation Act conflicts with current policy. We wish to mention only two. With the elimination of rail passenger service the public's ability to choose among different modes of transportation is being restricted. This would not be such a serious situation if the various methods of transportation were perfect substitutes. They are not. They are in many ways complementary but not substitutive. Therefore the mobility of the public is being lessened and the cost of maintaining the same amount of mobility is being increased.
Secondly, the elimination of rail passenger service is promoting the increased use of automobiles at the same time as the public and various levels of Government are becoming concerned about the increasing costs of pollution, congestion, etc. The current policy is encouraging the elimination of rail passenger service despite the knowledge that such service is the most acceptable means of moving large numbers of people on an urban, interurban and national basis. We submit that the aims of the present policy of the National Transportation Act are outdated, inadequate, and inappropriate and should therefore be immediately revised.
I could read much more, because I certainly concur with a good part of it. In terms of Atlantic Canada, not only have we not moved ahead to implement the firm recommendations of the four Atlantic premiers or of the Atlantic transportation committee, but on a national basis there is a question whether we should review some of the underlying principles of the national transportation policy.
In the few minutes I have remaining, I should like to mention the question of re-financing in a very general way because it is a very complicated subject. It appears that the minister's statement can be taken at face value and we will have another opportunity in another session, if and when there is another session, to discuss other features of the Canadian National Railways or Air Canada. The minister said there will be a bill to separate Air Canada from the CNR and also that there will be, I believe he said, a new CNR revision act. I think members should take note now that in any so-called revision act we should not continue to perpetuate the myth about the debt structure of the CNR, notwithstanding the debt structure it assumed many years ago in respect of all the other railways. I do not have the time or expertise today to go into this in any great detail, but in 1952 there was a recapitulation of the CNR debt structure which involved hundreds of millions of dollars. At that time, and through that bill, as a result of the buying of shares and the low interest placed on some of the loans, the CNR was sup-
April 21, 1972

posed to be put on a position to compete with any other railway. It was felt then, that the CNR would not need to come back perpetually to the Parliament of Canada to be bailed out.
It will be very interesting when the new bill is introduced to see just what explanation will be given concerning why the taxpayers of Canada will again have to bail out the CNR because of the very heavy debt structure that has been criticized since 1952. This question has a real impact upon anyone involved in the trucking industry, because as we all know both CP and CNR carry on very large trucking operations. In the case of CP it is through Smith's Transport, and in the case of CN it is through CNCL and a host of similar companies which carry out the motor transportation operation.
The CN has not differentiated between these two aspects of its operations to the point where we can ascertain what costs are charged against rail and what costs are charged against motor transportation. This is a situation we should check into when the recapitalization bill comes before the House.
The measure before us will, if passed, perpetuate a situation in which motive transport is subsidized from the public purse despite the fact that this section of the railway company's operation is in direct competition with private trucking companies. It is one thing for CN or CP to be in the trucking business. That may be fine. But there are many other companies in the trucking business across Canada, and we are giving CN an unfair advantage if we enable it to get money from the public purse either by means of an annual financing bill such as is before us, or by way of the recapitalization bill which the minister talked about.
I hope that before the bill comes to a vote on second reading, steps will be taken to refer this matter to the transport committee in order that the proposals of the CNR can be examined by that body in a context which would allow representatives of the trucking industry and others concerned to cross-examine the railway company on its proposals. We might as well admit that members of the transport committee of this House do not possess the expertise necessary to carry out an effective cross-examination of the company officials in this area or to become involved in the complex financial operations of the CN. Nor can this be expected of hon. members, bearing in mind all the other claims on their time in discharging their various duties.
Even the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) would, I am sure, admit his inadequacy when it comes to following through the maze of CN financing, beginning with the fact that it is not possible to distinguish between expenditures chargeable to the trucking side of the enterprise and those chargeable to the rail operation. It is too complex for ordinary people to understand.
