speechtext:
This is too serious a matter to be approached in a partisan way. This is a problem which has affected governments of all political stripes. I believe that before any recapitalization bill is considered by the transport committee we should have the benefit of a public hearing before the CTC where people more knowledgeable than we are can form an opinion as to the need for any such refinancing measure. After all, the CN was refinanced in 1952 and at that time the then president, Donald Gordon, took the view that there would be no need for the company to return to parliament in the hope that once again the taxpayers would bail out the company.
I should now like to say one or two things about Air Canada. First, I do not believe that we in Atlantic Canada have complained sufficiently about the plan to remove freight service personnel out of Halifax and locate them in Montreal, assisted by a computer service to advise them as to the vagaries of weather. We who live in Atlantic Canada know that one place can be in bright sunshine while another just a mile down the road is in thick fog. I suggest that Air Canada will find out to its embarrassment that no matter where it may locate these service personnel and no matter what computers are used, the service will not be as good as if it were provided on the spot, particularly when we are talking about coastal weather conditions, the strangest weather conditions of all to predict.
Everyone in Ottawa knows about the difficulties which arise when trying to get a reservation on an airplane after a certain hour. I have been trying today to get a reservation for a flight to Halifax. I was informed of the prerecorded signal from the computer located in Montreal, or wherever it is, but I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the reservations service is still not as good as it was when the office was here in Ottawa. And this is a relatively mechanical, administrative process. What will happen when an attempt is made to predict weather conditions? A few days ago I left my riding in bright sunshine. When I got to Halifax airport, 60 miles away, I found that the airport was fogbound and that no traffic was moving. On one occasion I telephoned Air Canada to ask about the weather situation in Halifax and was told that planes were flying, that everything was all right. After a four-hour drive in foul conditons, I arrived at the airport to find the runways fogbound and no traffic moving.
Nowadays, when I want information about weather conditions I telephone the airport directly. In light of this and similar experiences I believe it is a retrograde step to move service personnel to another location, as Air Canada proposes to do. I believe the travelling public will be far worse served after this change than it is at present.

April 21, 1972
CNR and Air Canada
Though my time is limited I should like to say a word or two about freight. I will tell hon. members a little story to illustrate in a personal way the problems with which shippers are confronted. For more than three months I had been trying to ship a box of books from my office to Halifax. The consignment is now somewhere between Ottawa and Halifax. I have spoken to people in Montreal in CN and in CP. They tell me there is no rail service into my area. I have asked my secretary to get me the names of the people who are telling me this garbage, in order that an appropriate letter can be written to higher officials in an attempt to ensure that something as simple as shipping a box of books to my area can be accomplished. I might add that it is a moderately progressive area, with mail service. I am trying to find out what all this hocus pocus is about.
Then, again, while I was in my constituency during the Easter recess I heard a complaint from a businessman that instead of being able to get deliveries by express within two or three days from Montreal he has to wait up to four weeks for shipments which are vital to his business as a user of aluminum products which are sent to him in broken lots. Regardless of what grand proposals the minister may have in mind, it is questions like these which deserve prompt consideration. In addition, of course, there is the question of increases in rates. The question of rate increases must be studied so we can maintain access to central Canadian markets.
Secondly, I think the minister could do what was done in the west when we were worried about supplying boxcars to carry grain and there was pressure to get the grain to the coast. At certain times they had what was called a controller at Winnipeg, or wherever these men work, to expedite or co-ordinate the movement of boxcars so that the demand for grain could be met. I do not know whether to call such a person a co-ordinator or an expediter, but as a matter of service by the government to the people of Atlantic Canada we should have express shipments made in less than the two to four weeks that they presently take. My area is serviced by the DAR-the Dominion Atlantic Railway-a subsidiary of the CPR. There is a problem in obtaining transfers from the CN to the DAR, which is why it became known as the "Dangerous And Rotten". This is where the tie-ups occurred.
I notice my time has just about expired, but I hope the minister will seriously study the proposals of the Atlantic premiers which have not so far been implemented. Secondly, I hope he will follow the recommendations of the transport committee which have found blessing on all sides of the House. Thirdly, I hope the minister will set up a co-ordinator or expediter so that when a man pays for express service he gets it, thus being able to maintain his operation. Certainly this is difficult enough under the present trying conditions.

speakeroldname: Mr. John Roberts (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the chance to speak on this motion before the House because it gives me the opportunity to bring to its attention a very serious situation in the area generally north of Toronto. I refer to the complete lack of sensitivity of the

Canadian National, so far demonstrated, in regard to providing what is so badly needed in that area, namely, an efficient system of commuter transportation. This is an area where Canadian National Railways has singularly failed to meet its responsibility to the public and, more particularly, to the citizens of my area. Perhaps it would be useful to give some indication of the background to this problem to show the need and the desire for this service which so far the Canadian National has signally failed to provide.
I am talking of the area north of Toronto up as far as Lake Simcoe which north of the boundaries of metropolitan Toronto comprises well over 140,000 people. If we take into consideration those Canadians who are living within the boundaries of metropolitan Toronto but who could equally be served by such a commuter service, then we are talking of a population of roughly a quarter of a million people who have expressed for the last ten years, through every elected official at every level of government, no matter of which political persuasion, unanimous support for the provision of a commuter service. As I say, this support has been echoed by every community, village and social organization. So I suggest there is not much doubt about the desire of this population pool to use such a service. Nor is there much doubt about the facilities. There are, in fact, Canadian National Railways' lines operating through this area which are capable of providing a commuter service if only the railway itself were prepared to provide it. Even back as far as 1964 the metropolitan Toronto and region transportation study, through its researches, indicated a definite travel potential for such a service and, as well, a strong desire on the part of those in the area to use the service.
Over the past ten years the public demonstration of the need and desire to have such a service has been extremely clear. But what has been the reaction of the railways to this need? The reaction has been to try to shift responsibility. Every time the railways are asked to provide a service, they look over their shoulder and try to find somebody else to do it for them. First of all they shifted the responsibility onto the provincial government of Ontario. When we think of the eastern and western commuter services in and around Toronto, the Ontario government was prepared to take up this burden. Indeed, the provincial government committed itself to providing commuter service north of Toronto. When the province retracted from this commitment, the federal government at that stage became involved and took the initiative in promoting a tripartite study of commuter problems, a study involving the co-operation of the regional, provincial and federal governments.
Of course, this study takes time to complete. It also has implications not only for the Toronto area but for other areas of Canada. It will establish precedents regarding federal involvement in the provision of commuter services as well as for co-operation between provincial and federal governments and it will take all levels of government some time fully to consider these precedents. But this, Mr. Speaker, lies in the future.
What concerns me particularly is not future need and how it is to be serviced; what I am talking about is the need of the present population living in the area which for
April 21, 1972

well over a decade has indicated its desire for an improved service, for a commuter service. These people have waited a long time and with patience, perhaps too much patience. The result has been the ignoring of their need by Canadian National Railways-a lack, if you like, of social responsibility on the part of the CNR.
Faced with a magnificent opportunity to provide profitable services that would be useful to the citizens of the area, the CNR has done nothing. I am sure we have all known some people who, when they stumble across opportunity, immediately pick themselves up, brush themselves off and hurry on as quickly as they can, pretending that they never stumbled at all. That is exactly what the railways, particularly the CNR, have been doing in relation to providing commuter services-picking themselves up, avoiding the opportunity, hustling on and doing other things that they would prefer to do. Just what is the view of the railway? It seems to me that the CNR is just trying to make money, or perhaps you might say just trying to lose as little money as possible. It finds it more convenient to ship goods, or to run hotels-even if it has the Hilton hotel chain run them for them-than to meet the needs of the people, needs that the railways were established to meet.
I think it is woefully wrong for the CNR to pretend that it is just another commercial institution, as if it were making hula-hoops or bobby-pins. If it finds a more profitable area of activity than the provision of commuter transportation services, then it just ignores the need for those transportation services. I suggest that the CNR exists not just to make money but to provide a service to the people of Canada. Certainly that is what it was chartered by parliament to do.
What has been the reaction of the CNR? What are its motives? It is hard to deal with motives as distinct from looking at what in fact has happened. The CNR has not been concerned with the provision of services that might be needed; and if any evidence were required in order to show they are needed I might cite the example of the Markham service which passes close to my constituency. The CNR resisted for a long time the provision of passenger services to the people in that area. Then when the Canadian Transportation Commission required them to do so, the railway found it had more business than it was prepared for. The CN were surprised at the number of passengers who wanted the service, which I suggest is a demonstration of real need and user potential.
Recently we have heard reports that the CNR is planning to close down the station at Stouffville, which would be vitally needed for a commuter service. Fortunately, yesterday in our discussion of the estimates before the committee on transportation it was made fairly clear by Mr. Pickersgill that there will be no reduction or closing of facilities at Stouffville which would in any way harm the passenger service.
We are not asking the CNR to do something unique, unheard of or never done anywhere else in Canada. There is a commuter service provided in the Montreal area. That service has been provided for well over 50 years. I suspect this service is provided at a profit, otherwise surely the
CNR and Air Canada
CNR would get rid of it since commuter services are not imposed on the railway by the transportation acts. If they can make money on commuter services around Montreal, or break even, why can they not provide similar services at the break-even point in and around Toronto?
The lack of desire on the part of the CNR to meet its responsibilities in relation to commuter passengers is one of the reasons I presented Bill C-24 to the House. That bill would establish a commuter passenger authority in and around the province of Ontario. It is because the CNR has not been conscious of its social responsibility that I have taken what is to some extent the drastic step of suggesting to the House of Commons that a new authority be established which would take into account, more effectively than is now being done, the need for commuter services in the Toronto area.
The tendency of the CNR has been constantly to hide behind the railway and transportation acts by saying that what is described there as the responsibility of the railways will be interpreted by them as the maximum of what they will do. It is true that when those acts were written it was not foreseen as strongly as it is today that there would be such a need for commuter services in and around urban areas of this country. These acts concentrate more on passenger service and place restrictions and limitations on the ability of the railways to get out of existing services, rather than concentrating upon the need for provision of new services.
I suggest as strongly as I can that it is wrong for the railways to say that what is the minimum required by law is the most they will do. That was hardly the kind of adventurous spirit that motivated the original railwaymen of this country to develop our country through the provision of an adequate transportation system. It is not even a businesslike attitude for any company, when given the opportunity, to resolutely refuse to take advantage of it because it is not required to do so by existing acts.
There is no doubt the CNR has the power to provide these services if it wishes to do so. My belief is that it would be profitable for it to do so. One would like to see the CNR much more forthcoming in meeting the legitimate needs of the population rather than concentrating too strongly simply on those things which are most convenient and profitable to it.
I hope that later in this session I will have the chance to discuss much more fully than I can this afternoon the needs I have described today and how they can be met effectively by Bill C-24. My purpose in speaking this afternoon is to bring attention to the House, as forcefully as I can, and to Canadian National Railways, the railway's responsibility to the commuter passengers-a need they are not now meeting but which I believe is a requirement this House should place upon them.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, two great transportation companies, Air Canada and the Canadian National Railways, are once again trying to obtain the authorization to use respectively $219,800,000 and 114 million dollars for their financial operations in various areas: transactions, development, payment of

April 21, 1972
CNR and Air Canada
bonds and new investment, including reserves for any deficiency in operating revenues until June 30, 1972.
I quite realize that corporations of the size of Air Canada and the Canadian National Railways are prepared to proceed with financial transactions from time to time, and I hope that this use of capital will be beneficial. Transportation in all its forms will always be with us.
Presently, we see that railway companies are testing various administrative procedures, and their officials claim that the objective is to show a profit. Unfortunately, that so-called modernization has resulted until now in massive lay-offs. Forecasts create a climate of insecurity among numerous workers who have given regular and valuable services to railway companies during many years.
As for results, I can point out certain facts of which the Canadian people are aware anyway, for instance, the increase in derailments, the downgrading of the passenger service through the removal of stops in convenient places. And I might even add the complete removal of train runs which would have been profit-earning, had the authorities been wise enough to take the advice of conductors before setting time-tables.
In our area, for instance, when the question of abolishing trains nos. 122 and 123, in the Chaleurs area, came up, the fact that our area was under a social and economic development program in which the population had been invited to take part, was ignored. Now, an important company like the CNR is negating every effort made over the past several years to bring together the different partners: governments, private decision making centres, and the population, refusing to take part in development projects and admitting casually that it has made a unilateral decision that could have consequences on the present experiment.
Yet, had its schedule been better balanced, the train could have run again during the holidays; and if some cared enough, it could be done immediately. If efforts are made to improve the service, there is no reason why it could not be profitable.
At this stage in my remarks, I want to point out one thing because derailments are increasing and the situation is becoming serious. Let us recall, for instance, that of the Rapido which occurred in early March, at Mile 33.3 near Joly in the riding of Lotbiniere, and caused the death of a family head. That accident was caused by the negligence of the authorities whose responsibility it was to make decisions about snow removal on that track. It is easy to conclude that the accident was caused by bad weather, but any serious observer will admit that a snowplough should have been used to remove the snow from the track before the train went through.
The maintenance staff is kept to a minimum in a misguided attempt to save money, and we have to mourn the death of an assistant engineer leaving a wife and three children.
The government sits back and waits. The situation is gradually deteriorating in the rail passenger service. The government is apparently ready to authorize them to

make various transactions, without making the necessary investigations which would undoubtedly reveal administrative mistakes which should be corrected. It might even be possible to find out one day what is the cause of those difficulties.
I have asked for a thorough investigation respecting the CNR's administrative procedures and I have not been the only one to do so. That is why I do not want to miss this opportunity to point out to the Minister of Transport and to the other members that it would be time to put some order in that bureaucratic organization.
Orders coming from management multiply, sometimes with prejudicial results. Here are some examples. In early February 1972, that is not long ago, about 350 mail bags of a total of 500 shipped to Levis, Quebec City and the area failed to be delivered because the employees assigned to that type of job were short of time. Orders issued by management set the train departure, with the result that the mail delivery suffered considerable delays. Those mail bags were carried clear across the province then back again and in some cases the delays greatly inconvenienced the addressees.
According to the information I got from reliable sources, such orders from management are no longer considered as errors but as a bad habit with disastrous consequences.
As for decisions to close down stations, most of the time they are based on an automatic command system whose efficiency has yet to be proven. This modern information system no doubt entails various inconveniences. One would not imagine that computers can replace men in all fields. Quite often, we are victimized by delays and errors though our era is one of mechanized robots. Fortunately, they are not hurt by the communicable fevers or the epidemic strikes that we are experiencing.
Among the reasons justifying a real inquiry, I have already mentioned the derailments that are multiplying at an alarming rate. A short survey of the statistics on this area is convincing. If we are to prevent accidents, strict control and regulations should be established for railways.
It happens too often that railway management is quite astonishingly ignoring railway operations. Economic matters are given priority over security with the results we all know.
Without saying that derailments are due to administrative inefficiency, since various factors sometimes create unforeseeable situations, I maintain that a fair number of them are attributable to exaggerated reductions in maintenance personnel.
The railway representatives say that this reduction was made essential because of technology and that the rails which used to be 39 feet long are now welded over 1,200 to 1,500 feet. Consequently, the rail joints may be checked much faster. Sleepers are made of hardwood processed to last 30 to 40 years, embankments have been widened by a few feet, gravel has been replaced by crushed stone and these are so many factors which should ensure better safety provided the maintenance and surveillance personnel is adequate and judiciously posted and thus in a position to make the required verifications.
April 21, 1972

No sensible observer will be easily convinced that railway maintenance may be carried out by a team of truckers however well-intentioned.
In order to provide some public explanations regarding the problem of derailments, I would say that they are the result of a lack of co-ordination between locomotive and railway car manufacturers and the companies which use this rolling stock. It is acknowledged that there is an imbalance somewhere. This is a valid reason for the representatives of various areas of the country to point out what they deem to be administrative mistakes that should be rectified prior to the adoption of legislation authorizing the provision of moneys to meet certain capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railways system.
Another important item which cannot be ignored when we speak of the administrative services of the CN is the question of indebtedness. Any firm which has to set aside $75 million of its annual operating income for servicing its debts, should admittedly be allowed a certain period of time "to juggle" with figures.
Under the heading of "General", on page 4 of the Canadian National Railways annual report for 1970, it is said that the Canadian National handled a larger volume of business in 1970 than in the previous year and was able to produce increased revenues from nearly all major services. However, the cost of doing business continued to mount as a result of higher wage rates and higher prices for materials and services. Some freight rate increases- applied within the price restraint guidelines set by the Prices and Incomes Commission-plus effective control of expenses and improved productivity enabled CN to offset part of the higher costs.
Following the table showing the revenue increase or decrease as compared with that of 1969, the report continues, and I quote:
The net income before interest on debt-that is, the "operating profit" of the Company-was $45.8 million in 1970. This was lower than in 1969. But it can be considered a good achievement in a year characterized by a slowdown in the economy, strikes in the automobile and pulp and paper industries, and a slackening in demand for automobiles and for lumber and other construction materials, as well as the annual reduction in payments related to the National Transportation Act.
Gross revenues from railway and other CN operations reached $1,167.7 million, the highest in the history of the Company.
On page 6, there is a statement of the amounts of interest due on the debt, and I quote:
Net interest on debt amounted to $75.5 million, an increase of $1.3 million over 1969.
This is rather serious!
As I suggested, following an investigation into the various CN administrative services, it might be possible to find a way to consolidate this debt through long-term loans with as low a rate of interest as possible-something along the lines of loan terms granted to underdeveloped countries.
In Canada, we had the advantage of experiencing several forms of development. Unfortunately, the financial system which creates debts has become an obstacle to our development, with the consequence that many enter-
CNR and Air Canada
prises-our country for one-are faced with the problem of unpaid and unpayable debts.
Even some of our so-called expert administrators feel they are doing quite well when they manage to pay nothing but the interest on the huge debts that are getting bigger. One can easily imagine what would happen if all the citizens had the same approach.
Taking into account the situation and the need to provide passenger service, the Transport Department should look more closely into the decisions made by the management of transportation companies and give the people adequate service.
In closing my remarks, I should like to read from an article that is much to the point, which contains a great deal of facts that sometimes agree and sometimes disagree with the approach taken by the management of our railways. I shall quote an article by Mr. Marice Huot published in Montreal-Matin on February 15, 1972.
-the service has alarmingly deteriorated. Does that mean that it could not be improved? We suggest that it can be, if we use our imagination in order to provide passengers with the service they are entitled to expect. In the United States, the passenger transportation service has been put into operation again for some time. Many old outmoded cars were restored, their inside decorated, children playrooms were made out of freight cars which can be coupled on to ordinary trains, such as trains of people going on holiday, thus enabling some families to travel with their children in a more human and more comfortable way. Tracks are improved thanks to more careful maintenance. They changed their staff's uniforms, hired smiling stewardesses like on planes, provided for entertainment such as movies and TV near large centres. Those trains also carry cars of people who appreciate not having to drive over long distances but who use their car once they are arrived. In other words, it is a whole new rail philosophy which has been started in order to make rail travel more competitive, instead of always speaking of abadoning lines, not because they could not be profitable, but because they were made unprofitable through remissness. Henceforth, we should attract the travelling public with pleasure trains. We should make travelling by train a pleasant experience and not a sort of punishment. Let us put as much effort into restoring passenger lines as we do for freight traffic and railway transportation will gain new lustre and activity. In sea transportation the trend is towards cruises; railways also could plan cruises on wheels if they got organized accordingly.
So, I think that Department of Transport officials should keep a close watch on how CNR management plans schedules and makes decisions without consultations, which is far from beneficial to Canadian residents who would sometimes wish to use railway services.
Besides , I was told recently again, "Try to inquire whether there are not people in the management of the CNR who have interests in bus or other means of transportations, as it would seem, from their attitude, that they are interested in people giving up the railway and using other modes of transportation.
I therefore hope the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) will look after the matter and that we can be assured of having a passenger transport service suitable for the population which has already paid a great deal for it.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the measure before us this afternoon, Bill C-4, authorizes the provision of

April 21, 1972
CNR and Air Canada
moneys to meet certain capital expenditures of the CNR system and Air Canada. I would like to say a few words today about the problem of strikes in regard to Air Canada and our airports and some of the conclusions to which I have come, very reluctantly, but which nevertheless I am sure are shared by many Canadians.
It has been a principle with me, as with many Canadians, that the right to strike is a basic right of a democratic society. The right to withhold one's services from the labour market is one that has been built, by our law and customs, into a right which has been respected by all Canadians. There have been problems in connection with the development of this policy: it has not been developed very easily. Resistance to this approach has been very strongly allied to the concept that the right to strike is a fundamental right. But like many rights, it also has responsibilities.
At this stage I want to say a few words about some of the problems that are raised by strikes which have taken place. Whether it is an airline pilots' strike, an air traffic controllers' strike, or the radar technicians who provide service to airports, and whether the employer happens to be with the Department of Transport or Air Canada is really incidental to the purposes for which I want to speak today.
I wish to quote from two letters I received from constituents. The first one is from L. A. McKeown who resides at 473 Mayfair Avenue, in this city. I have chosen this letter because I think it is typical and because I believe the opinions expressed in it are shared by many. It reads:
I would like to suggest that you re-examine the whole question of the right to strike. In extending this right to strike to essential services you have built the premise on false grounds. The right to strike is not a prime right. There are other rights which have higher priority. When a low priority right runs counter to a high priority right then the lower priority right has to give way.
For instance, national safety has a higher priority than the right of free speech. In the same way private rights have to be tempered when they run contrary to the public good. The freedom to act in any way by any two parties is limited only to the extent that they carry out this liberty in their own back yard and do not impede the liberty of others to carry out their normal and rightful duties. In other words, it has been considered so far permissible for a disagreement to exist between a private employer and employees of that company. The rights of disinterested third parties are usually not greatly inconvenienced too much in such a dispute. For instance, the General Motors strike about 15 months ago meant that I had to buy a Chrysler or Ford product rather than a General Motors product. However, when you give a monopoly to some group then you no longer have the choice of getting a Chrysler or a Ford. One of the responsibilities that a monopoly carries with it is that the monopoly guarantees to provide some particular product or service according to specification and that this security from competition is in return for the contracted monopoly.
The problem here relates to specific groups, in many cases small in number, and the amount of damage they are able to inflict on the public generally. I would also like to quote from a letter which I received from H. Lee Briggs, 2070 Dovercourt Avenue, in the city of Ottawa, as follows:
Perhaps the issues are most readily identified in the recent strike by the Air Traffic controllers union. In this connection let us try to establish some kind of a financial balance, in the knowledge that dollars are far from everything.
Two years ago there were about a thousand air controllers. On last January 17, 1,750 controllers went on strike. They had largely been trained at the expense of Canadian taxpayers for 141 months during which training time they received pay at rates between $4,900 and $5,500 per year. Their school training cost the government $4,700 per graduate.
He cites his source of this information.
Prior to strike, pay rates ranged AI-1, min. $6,962, to AI-9, max. $18,460. I am guessing the average rate of pay on January 17 to be $14,000. DOT payroll (including 23 per cent benefits?) would be some $3 million.
Strike demands were for a 60 per cent increase . . . plus a work week reduction from 35 down to 30 hours. This is $1,800,000 more pay to existing controllers, plus $260,000 for more people. Their demands, then, are $2,060,000. But let us say that they could be willing to finally settle for a mere $1 million. So we have 1,750 DOT employees, $3 million payroll, $1 million minimum demand to go back to work.
Now, Mr. Francis, look what has happened to Canada. Absolutely all commercial flights in or to Canada shut down. Air Canada net loss alone $2 million. Air Canada laid off 10,000 ticket agents, clerficals and related employees at the outset. Air Canada then laid off, 1,000 more of the same. Air Canada cut pay of 3,200 management level employees by 40 per cent. ..
One estimate of Air Canada pay cut off, $2,500,000.
Then he sums it up rather concisely, Mr. Speaker.
I, a mild mannered conformist from your constituency-
I think he is modest in his description of himself.
-am constrained to ask the Members of the Parliament of Canada, how does each one of you justify this bloody nonsense:
1,750 DOT employees, vs. A loss to the Canadian economy of Payroll $3 million.	$60 to $100 million, untold massive
Strike demands initi- inconveniences, tremendous waste of ally $1.8 million.	time and effort, layoffs everywhere,
pay stoppages, business thwarted except at higher cost, Canada chopped into small segments in midwinter.
My colleague, the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Orange), described the great hardship suffered by the outlying parts of Canada in the exercise of this so-called right to strike which up to this point I have supported in my public life almost without qualification.
In the Globe and Mail this morning a former premier of the province of Ontario was quoted regarding exactly the same subject. He talked in terms of the right to strike of teachers and asked the fundamental question of whether our society is such that teachers can go on strike and say that our children will not be educated until their demands are met. Where does this concept fit into a civilized society? I am not a simplistic person, Mr. Speaker. I have been head of a staff association in the public service and I believe that the right to strike is essential in democratic society in certain circumstances. But I say that in this forum-I know I say it with the agreement of a large number of people in this country-the right to strike by a small number of employees in certain critical areas has to be reconsidered.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I see that only a few minutes are left before private members' hour and this will not permit me to deal with all the matters I would like to discuss in the debate on the CN financing bill. Some people may wonder why, when the CN financing bill is presented to the House each year, a fairly lengthy debate takes place. I think this happens because of the importance of railways to Canada and the widespread operations of Canadian National Railways in particular. Railways have played an important part in the development of this country since confederation.
During this debate many suggestions have been made for improvement in the operation of the CNR. Hon. members have voiced complaints about its inadequacies. We cannot discuss CN operations and financing, however, unless we look at the over-all operation of railways in Canada, which brings us to consideration of the operations of CPR. It is my view that many of the basic problems of railway transportation in Canada cannot be solved until we have a government with the courage and wisdom to nationalize the CPR and the industrial empire which has resulted from generous grants made when its operations commenced. I think this is the basic step which must be taken, and I think the Canadian people are ready for it. But we need a government with the courage to take such a step which would be in the interest of all Canadians.
One other aspect of railway transportation must be considered during a debate such as this. That is the importance of developing a policy to equalize transportation rates across the country. This matter is of increasing importance because of the development taking place in our economy. A great deal has been said about regional disparities. In my opinion, one of the major contributing factors to this problem is the inequity in transportation costs. It is high time that the National Transportation Act and its concept adopted over the years was scrapped and we developed a policy to equalize transportation costs.
I see that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) is in his seat. On a number of occasions he has stated that the government is working on an industrial strategy, whatever that might be. A good deal has been said about it, but I shall not go into that matter in detail. However, I think there is general agreement that we need a greater degree of strategy and focus on priorities of industrial development and growth in Canada in the future. We cannot deal with this question, however,
Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act
unless we also deal with the problem of inequities in transportation costs in Canada.
If we allow the present structure of transportation costs to remain while we develop a new industrial strategy, those regions which already face higher transportation costs than others will still be discriminated against. I suggest that some regions of Canada will suffer under any industrial strategy that is developed unless at the same time there is a change in our transportation policy which will result in equalized transportation costs across the country. This is an important matter which should be noted by the government.

subtopic: TERRITORIAL SEA AND FISHING ZONES ACT
TERRITORIAL SEA AND FISHING ZONES ACT
subsubtopic: PROVISION TO DISTINGUISH FISHING ZONE FROM TERRITORIAL SEA OR INTERNAL WATERS
speechtext:
that Bill C-ll, to amend the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act, be read a second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to come to the House today to discuss Bill C-ll. I have presented this bill on a number of occasions. It was introduced in the first session of this parliament, shortly after I was elected, as Bill C-189, in the second session as Bill C-91, and in the third session as Bill C-195-and now it is Bill C-ll. My reason for presenting it every session since this parliament began is that despite certain developments which have taken place since 1968, of which hon. members are aware, there is still need to improve our fisheries legislation and to define the limits which constitute Canada's fishing zones.
Before proceeding further I wish to thank two members of the Pacific Trollermen's Association, Dick Williams of the vessel Seabeam and his former deckhand, Mr. Meadows, who assisted me over the years with this bill and who took me out on the commercial fishing bank so that I might better understand the point of view and problems of the fishermen. I also wish to thank the fishermen of the west coast for circulating a petition which I presented to parliament two years ago in support of Bill C-91, which is the same bill as the one before us today. That petition, with 33,000 names appended, was the largest petition, I believe, ever to be presented to this parliament. These fishermen played an important part in persuading the government to bring in legislation in this area, specifically the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act of 1970, which has improved the situation over what it was previously

April 21, 1972
Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act although not to the point that my friends who fish off the west coast of Canada would wish.
I might also mention that the bill has the full support of the Fisheries Association of Canada which, at its annual meeting in 1971, went on record and resolved that Canada, at the 1973 Law of the Sea Conference, should maintain the position that anadromous species of fish are the property of the country of origin and that-
-the ownership of the creatures on and over the continental shelf and slope is vested in the coastal state which is responsible for establishing the regime for conservation and management of those stocks and the fisheries thereon.
That is the point of my bill, namely, extending our present limits for exclusive fishing zones, or exclusive fisheries management zones, from the limit presently set out to the end of the continental shelf. There are difficulties because international law recognizes many definitions of the term "continental shelf." One definition suggests that you can go out until you reach the 200-fathom mark; the second-again artificial-that you go out to the 1,000-fathom mark. A third definition suggests that you should go out until the continental shelf drops Off at a certain angle, a number of degrees. Still another definition is that you must consider actual differences in the quality of the seabed and thus determine where the continental shelf ends; that you can tell from the seabed when you come to the edge of the continental shelf and slope. Whatever is decided ultimately, I think that for the purposes of this bill we can safely say that we will go for the limit that is most realistic, which is 1,000 fathoms. We think that is where the continental slope incline increases and that is where the actual limit of the continental shelf ought to be.
The government, two years after I first introduced my bill, brought down the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act of 1970. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) made interesting comments in that debate which I should like to quote. On April 17, 1970, he said, as reported at page 6015 of Hansard:
I have made clear, as has the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), that we will not back down one inch from our basic position on sovereignty but there is no interest on the part of the Canadian government in the exercise of chauvinism.
I agree completely with the minister's approach. This bill is not intended to be chauvinistic and is not directed against any nation or group of nations. I feel, however, that this is perhaps the only way in which the resources of the continental shelf and slope, and in particular the anadromous species such as salmon and sea-going trout, or steelhead, can be properly protected. The Secretary of State for External Affairs also said, as reported at page 6016:
-the bill would, in keeping with the government's approach to the question, enable us to separate fisheries jurisdiction from the complete sovereignty which states exercise in their territorial sea and internal waters.
This bill is specifically directed to solving some of our difficulties off the west coast. There are some serious problems that have arisen in connection with fishing on the big bank just off Vancouver Island. Hon. members will recall that on a number of occasions Canadian fishermen were harassed by Russian vessels and prevented from fishing in that area. Furthermore, our fishermen were endangered by what I consider to be reckless practices on the part of the Russians. The upshot was that the

Canadian government eventually made an agreement with the Russian government limiting the use by Russian vessels in the waters off the west coast. The Russians agreed not to fish in a certain area. Although that agreement was not of major importance, at least it established a precedent. An agreement was reached with the Soviet government for limiting the activities of Russian fishing vessels off the coast of Vancouver Island beyond the 12-mile limit; in other words, outside the limits established by the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act of 1970. That agreement is particularly important from the point of view of conservation, and has been greatly discussed.
I will not discuss all the problems of the east which are associated with preserving Atlantic salmon. Today, hon. members opposite from the Maritimes asked questions on that very point. I think the situation in the Maritimes is potentially the same as that which exists on the west coast. Our salmon, too, spawn in Canadian and American streams. They, too, go to sea and perhaps join, we do not know where, with other salmon of Siberian and Japanese rivers. We do not know where they go; perhaps, one day, that will be discovered, just as it has been discovered that Atlantic salmon go off the coast of Greenland.
Perhaps when that discovery occurs, on the west coast we will have to consider the same sort of problem that is now being considered on the east coast, because perhaps then our resources will be damaged in the same way by high seas fishing outside our control. We feel that it is important, therefore, that we get going in Canada and establish the right of controlling, for conservation purposes, the species of our continental shelf areas before that happens. This, I know, will be a subject that will concern the Canadian delegation which will be taking part in the 1973 Law of the Sea Conference.
I was rather disappointed to read the article which the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), whom I see sitting opposite, wrote for a west coast fisheries magazine in which he declared that the Canadian position was detrimental to the interests of west coast fishermen. I ought to point out that while there is reason for concern, the minister is aware of the difficulty of the troll fishery off Vancouver Island and has made public statements on the subject. I quote from a press release in which the minister said:
It is fully recognized that a substantial part of the troll fishery off Vancouver Island takes place immediately outside the 12-mile territorial limit (within the outer limits of the continental slope)-
He went on to talk about the Atlantic salmon and pointed out that we must bear in mind that a substantial part of the Danish high seas fishery fishes just outside the 12-mile limit off Greenland. The minister's position is perfectly clear. I should like to read a letter which the minister sent to me. It is dated April 18, 1972, and reads in part:
Dear David:
This will acknowledge your letter of March 17, 1972, concerning offshore salmon fishing.
Canada's position at the forthcoming Law of the Sea Conference is still under development. For your information, I am enclosing a copy of a brief statement on the subject.
Yours sincerely,
Jack Davis
April 21, 1972

I believe it is important for people on the west coast to know that Canada's position is not firm, as has been erroneously reported, and that the minister is looking for ways to take into account the troll fishery which he mentioned in his press release and letter. I think that if we were able to accept the principle of my bill, which extends the limit for conservation purposes to the edge of the continental shelf, rather than fisheries closing lines plus the 12-mile limit which is in our present legislation, and if we accepted the extension of the principle that outside the present limits there may be areas of the continental shelf which should also be included, we could perhaps solve the difficulty which faces the minister in his attempt to reconcile Canada's position on the east and west coasts.
The bill before us, as I have said, is a proposal that the subject matter be sent to committee, because this is the best that can be hoped for from a private member's bill. I feel that this is a worth-while step toward achieving some sort of reconciliation of position which would be satisfactory to both east and west coast fishermen and would at the same time meet the very real needs of Canada to have a consistent position at the Law of the Sea Conference in 1973.
I believe the difficulties we have faced over the past four years on the west coast and on the east coast underline the need for Canada to continue toward progressive legislation in an effort to increase the area of its jurisdiction. I feel it would be quite fair to claim on behalf of the troll fishermen on the west coast, with their excellent petition to the House which I mentioned earlier, that they have had a large part in achieving the advances of the 1970 legislation. There has been a closure of many areas which formerly were open to people of all nations and which now are restricted to Canadians. I think this is a positive rather than a negative point, that is, that this extension of jurisdiction has allowed us to preserve resources in a way which I believe has been most beneficial to the species concerned.
Even if we extend our jurisdiction further, as I suggest in this bill, we can always permit the fishermen of other nations to come into our area under licence. It may be that they could fish certain species in which we are not interested. Hake is a good example on the west coast. It may be that we could work out co-operative arrangements with these fishermen to take a certain species in which they are more interested than us. The herring fishery is an example where the Japanese are involved. Japanese experts say when conditions are right, and they indeed suggest when the fishermen should set their nets because they know full well the use to which the product will be put in Japan and when the fish are in the best condition for catching.
When I speak of extending exclusive Canadian jurisdiction I do not necessarily mean exclusively for our Canadian fishermen. It may be a good idea to have others come in and help harvest the resources of the sea. If this were done properly, I can see no problem. However, it is necessary to have someone responsible for jurisdiction, regulation and licensing as well as for conservation and the scientific work which must be carried out prior to licensing or regulation.
Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act
At present we are in the unfortunate position on the high seas where what belongs to everybody belongs to nobody. No one is interested in doing the scientific work and in spending money, because the people who would benefit might be of another state. If we can extend our jurisdiction to take in our major producing areas, we can perhaps persuade the government to increase the amount of scientific effort. I am sure the government could be persuaded to do so. I feel that when considering this bill- I know I am repeating a point I made earlier-it is not necessary to be too concerned about whether or not at this stage we can define the continental limits. I do not believe it is important at this stage to get too lied up in how this could create other difficulties in respect of our fisheries. I do not believe that it would. However, I feel it is important at this stage to proceed on a principle which the minister himself is on record as favouring, which other parties are on record as favouring and which I have been putting forward in the House frequently over the past four years.
I believe this is a bill which is modest in scope. I believe if we proceed as suggested we can achieve the objective without causing too much difficulty in terms of international retaliation. I agree that it does break new ground. It has certain risks in particular risk to our markets, which I do not wish to minimize; but I feel that in general it is a good idea at this stage to proceed with this legislation, send it to committee and thrash out all the details which, unfortunately, during private members' hour at the end of a week, and perhaps at the end of a parliament, may be difficult to cover. I trust and hope it will be possible for all members to agree with the proposal I have made.

subsubtopic: PROVISION TO DISTINGUISH FISHING ZONE FROM TERRITORIAL SEA OR INTERNAL WATERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, frequently when members of parliament rise in this House of Commons to speak on an issue which involves the fisheries not all members become as excited about it as I do. Perhaps this is good. Judging from the exchange we have had today and the motivation behind it, we could be taking up all the time of the House of Commons on this issue.
With regard to this bill and the remarks of the hon. member who introduced it, we are involved in an issue which is very fundamental. Although the fishery was a primary industry of what was to become Canada, for a number of years people in the House of Commons have treated the word "fish" as some kind of a dirty, four-letter word which has no relevance and no place in the House of Commons of Canada. We have begun to realize the risk we run in the involvement of other nations in this resource, and that unless urgency is given to the matter we will lose one of the most important and precious resources of the Canadian nation.
The bill introduced by my friend from the most western part of the country hits at one of the most fundamental problems faced by Canada. We stand in this House of Commons day after day, and we stand in committee day after day discussing issues which scratch the surface of such problems as this, and it always bothers me that we do not have more response in a practical way, not only in this government of 1972 but governments of the past couple of decades. I do not say this because the present government is in power.

April 21, 1972
Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act
We have never received from Canada a full response on this very vital issue. I talk to a large number of young people from all across this nation as they visit this House, and also as I travel around the various parts of Canada. They are asking us to see that government responds to the real needs of the Canadian people. I am saying, for the record, that five years from now this government, which is in a position to do something about these problems, as well as the government which succeeds it, will be held responsible by the Canadian people unless we can get a more fundamental response to the major problems of the renewable marine resources of Canada.
The hon. member who preceded me was talking about extending the area of the fishing zones to include the extremities of the continental shelf. On the west coast, Mr. Speaker, the area of the continental shelf is rather small when compared with that of the continental shelf on the east coast. On the east coast it extends as far as 400 miles, and going back to 1944, I believe it was, various countries of the world-from that year until 1958-began to negotiate the rights of the coastal states with respect to the continental shelf.
It was agreed in 1958, in international law, that the continental shelf, as it was defined in the agreement of that year, would belong to the coastal state. So we have a unique situation where Canada owns the ocean floor out to the extremities of the continental shelf, as well as the air space above the water, yet we cannot establish any permanent claim to the resource between the water level and the bottom of the ocean. The result is that we have on the east coast almost every major nation in the world with a large fishing fleet daily harvesting our marine resources.
As hon. members listen to the east coast members from day to day they will learn a little about the problems facing this country. We have the Russian fishing fleet which is the largest fisheries predator on the east coast. A few weeks ago they were present with 75 large vessels. With their very sophisticated equipment, capable of detecting the exact movement of various marine species, they inhabit a fishing area and launch what we on the east coast call gang-fishing. To do this they lie abreast of each other, drop their very sophisticated fishing gear, and in a matter of weeks they clean out a whole area, including the spawning mud and the sands on the bottom of the ocean floor, thereby destroying the resources which should be there forever. This is what is happening on the east coast of Canada today, Mr, Speaker.
There is no need to talk to biologists to see what the results of these actions will be: one can talk to any fisherman. In January and February of 1972 the landings of fish by all the Newfoundland fishermen, with all their fishing gear-this includes the offshore fishermen with their dragging operation as well as the inshore fishermen with their longliners, their $50,000 boats, and the real inshore fishermen with their small boats-was exactly 50 per cent of what it was for the same period in 1971. If that is not of major concern to the Canadian people, then I think we are in the wrong country. I say that as a Newfoundlander.
Day after day we get up in the House of Commons to raise the question of Canada exercising some of the rights

it has as a coastal state. One of the rights Canada has which I should like to repeat for the record is that in 1958 at the Law of the Sea Conference at Geneva, the coastal state was given a particular right which stated that if the coastal state, after six months of negotiation with the nations fishing the resources on its continental shelf, could not arrive at a multilateral agreement on conservation and management, then that state had the right to unilaterally impose certain conservation measures.
The condition of exercising such a right was that first of all the state had to indicate there was serious depletion of various species. We know, for example, that on Georges Bank the haddock have disappeared to the extent that even the fisheries people themselves claim they do not expect the species to be replenished by natural process. This is an example of the total destruction of a species. It is a crime against our resources, yet we have the spectre of the Canadian government willing to stand by, despite all its talk about nationalism and foreign involvement in our country, and allow other nations to move in on our shores with sophisticated fishing gear and equipment and devastate our resources.
As a coastal state, Mr. Speaker, we have the right to impose certain conservation measures and we have the right to say to other nations that there are areas which shall not be fished during certain times of the year. We have the right to say there are certain species of fish which are not allowed to be touched because of the threat of depletion. We have the right to say there are certain areas in which we shall impose quotas and allow only certain catches of fish to be taken off our shores. Canada is not threatening to launch a naval war against these countries by merely exercising these rights. We are not forcing them from our coasts altogether. We are only, as a nation, saying that we are not willing to see our fisherman who settled this country back in 1497 placed in a position where their livelihood is completely destroyed.
Perhaps, more important, Canadians who understand the issue, particularly young Canadians, will not be willing to allow nations of the world, including Canada, to destroy for ever various species of fish off our shores. The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) has got to his feet day after day and has indicated that all these difficulties should await the Law of the Sea Conference. In 1968, when this government first took office, the minister said that a couple of years from now we would hold a Law of the Sea Conference and we would get to the bottom of the problem. We were later told it would be 1972; then 1973. We learned today, Mr. Speaker, there is a very good chance that the Law of the Sea Conference will not be held until 1975; that Canada and the various countries concerned have not even agreed on an agenda and that Canada has not yet settled the position it will present at the Law of the Sea Conference even though a little country like Iceland has already printed in detailed form from its parliament the position they will take at the next Law of the Sea Conference.
There is another matter which ought to be realized. Even if we held the Law of the Sea Conference tomorrow morning, the matter of fisheries and renewable resources would find itself at the bottom of the totem pole because other areas of concern, such as the problems arising from
April 21, 1972

jurisdiction-the rights of coastal states in these areas- matters of pollution, matters of the disposition of weaponry, and so on, in the coastal areas would find themselves in a position of top priority. We are saying to the Minister of Fisheries and to the people of Canada that this matter has to receive more attention than is now paid to it.
We are also very much aware that the matter of fisheries is not a political issue in this country. We have seven members of parliament from the province of Newfoundland, which I represent, four from Prince Edward Island, 11 from Nova Scotia and ten, I believe, from New Brunswick. We have 37 members from the Atlantic region and six or seven from the province of Quebec-perhaps more than that-and the Gaspe area. The hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Bechard) might put the number on record. So we have about 40 members directly concerned with the fisheries.
We are having trouble in the House of Commons and in Canada generally in attracting national attention to a matter which vitally affects the issue of our territorial sovereignty. Unless we can get the Canadian people, particularly members of the government, to respond more readily we shall never get action this year despite the fact that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) is aware of the problem and is concerned about it. In spite of this awareness and concern, he is still not willing to place this question in a position of priority. The Minister of the Environment is not willing to place it in a position of priority. It doesn't have political sex appeal across the Canadian nation; it is not the sort of thing which will "turn on" people in Toronto.
This is a sad story, because regardless of how relevant the issue is-and the Minister of the Environment knows well the consequences of letting this issue go unresolved- we are not going to get action because we have been unable to sell the issue as a major national problem. We cannot get the House of Commons to pay full attention to it because the issue is not one which lends itself to this type of forum. We cannot go into great detail about the type of problems we face because there are so many other issues.
The members of the press, I say with respect, perhaps do not understand the depth or the breadth of the issues and the details involved. We could get up and talk for weeks about these matters, yet we would not get a sentence in the Globe and Mail, simply because this issue doesn't have the appeal to the readership of that newspaper. The sad story is that five or ten years from now Canadians will hang their heads in shame when they realize that the original great resource upon which Canada relied at its beginning has been so depleted that it has been crossed off as an economic issue in Canada.
It is shameful that we should stay here day after day and refuse to grapple with the problem. Today we had a typical response from the minister. We have had three examples over the last year which adequately demonstrate the lack of responsiveness of the minister to the Atlantic region. Let me say for the record that, despite the fact that this problem is so critical, the Minister of Fisheries has continually made changes in fisheries policy without any consultation with the Atlantic provinces or refer-
Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act ence to his directors and officials in federal offices in the Atlantic region.
Last year the minister was prepared to sign a treaty with the Norwegians which would have allowed them to harvest our resources of seals nine miles inside the 12-mile territorial limit. The minister indicated that this was a trade-off in order to get them out of the Gulf of St. Lawrence. A few weeks ago he introduced several treaties which had the effect of phasing out the operations of several other nations in the gulf. By as late as 1986 the French are to be out of the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Here again there has been no consultation with the provinces or reference to the officials in the Atlantic region.
If the minister were in the House this afternoon he would brag that this is an achievement. The fact is that by 1986 when the French leave the Gulf of St. Lawrence, the gulf will be as dead as the Sea of Gallilee as far as fish are concerned: there will be absolutely no fish left in the Gulf of St. Lawrence.
Today we had an example of the sort of response we get from the minister who has publicly stated that he will eliminate the Atlantic fishery. We know that the Danes have been harvesting salmon on the high seas since 1965, when the famous incident, which has been well quoted both in this House and in recent articles in the press, occurred regarding the discovery of the feeding ground of the Atlantic salmon. Ever since that time we have brought this matter to the attention of the government almost daily, but we cannot get any proof at all that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has laid any material of a substantial nature before the Danes to convince them of our concern.
The minister says that the problem must be resolved through negotiation. We recognize that we are not going to declare war on Denmark, but has the minister on behalf of the government forcefully told the Danes that we are not satisfied with their actions and will adopt certain procedures against them if they will not toe the line? It is Denmark that is the guilty party here. That is the country that is sick, yet the minister is deciding to perform surgery on Canada to cure the illness. We all know there is something rotten in Denmark, but we do not have to amputate the salmon fishery in the Atlantic region to prove the point.
The contention of the minister is that if we cut off salmon fishing in the Atlantic region we will prove to the Danes that we are interested in conservation. Let me tell the Minister of Fisheries, through you, Mr. Speaker, that it will be a frosty Sunday in the Atlantic region when the minister gets our approval of that policy. We will not go along with any such insidious recommendation, one that is born out of an abominable ignorance of the fisheries in our region. We need the support of the Canadian people for our problems.
Several weeks ago there was an incident of intimidation off our coast. I am glad to say that the people of British Columbia did the Canadian people proud last year when they responded to intimidation by a Russian vessel that attempted to ram, or perhaps did even ram one of our vessels. The people of the area and the fisherman came

Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act together and proved that together they were a force to be reckoned with. Unfortunately, our people did not respond recently in the same way. However, we have brought to the House accounts of several incidents in the last few weeks involving Russian fishing vessels off the east coast of Canada intimidating our fishing vessels. One vessel, the Zonnemaire-I forget the name of the captain-narrowly escaped being rammed and chopped in two by one of these great Russian fishing vessels off the southeast coast of Newfoundland.
We asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) if they would be prepared to make official representations to the Soviet Union, and I do not know whether anything has been done since. The only thing done of which we do have proof is that the director of fisheries for the Newfoundland area went out in the small boat, that is considered to be a patrol boat but would not survive the Rideau canal on a breezy day, and hove alongside the Russian vessel for three days in an attempt to board the vessel to make an official protest, but the Russians would not even allow the official on board.
Then the vessel had to return and a wire was sent to the Russian vessel stating, "We protest". The director of fisheries indicated that we were protesting their aggression and the Russians wired back, "We have received your telegram," full stop. To me, Mr. Speaker, this is a disgrace. If this incident had occurred anywhere else in the world there would have been a manifestation of grave concern against the aggressor nation. In our case, the director of fisheries at the local level manifests his concern. This is why the people of the Atlantic region are absolutely fed-up.
I am sure that if the Canadian people understood the magnitude and seriousness of the problem and how critical it is to the Atlantic region, they would support any government that showed a little muscle and exercised some control over our resources. The bill presented by the hon. member from British Columbia is a good one. We would like to see something similar along these lines for the east coast of Canada presented by the government. Unless we do, as a governing group we will be held guilty over the next four or five years for the continuing destruction of this very vital resource.

subsubtopic: PROVISION TO DISTINGUISH FISHING ZONE FROM TERRITORIAL SEA OR INTERNAL WATERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in support of the bill introduced by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Anderson). I might say in passing, and in a kindly way, that if he should find himself introducing this bill again in another session I hope he will do something to update the explanatory notes and put them in line with the amendments made to the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act of 1970. The principle of the bill is a very simple one, as the hon. member said when introducing it, namely, that we should establish the principle that our fishing zones extend to the outer edge of the continental shelf.
I should also like to say a few words of congratulation to the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundri-gan) who has just given us one of his usual vigorous speeches. My observation of him is that he has added a good deal of backbone to the position of the official oppo-

sition when it comes to fishery matters since he has been in the House.
I recall that in 1964, when the territorial seas and fishing zones bill was introduced, some of us were finding that we had a government which appeared to be nothing but a jellyfish when it came to speaking up on such matters. Unfortunately, we discovered at that time that the spokesmen for the official opposition were very much like jellyfish too. This has always been a matter of great regret to me, because I think that if those of us in this party had had the kind of vigorous support for the point of view just outlined by the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate at that time, we might have been able to convince the government to go a bit further than it did in 1964.
However, I can say at once that I have a very obvious reason for indicating my support for the bill introduced by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich. I placed an almost identical proposal before this House in the form of a report stage amendment to the government bill of 1970. In order to clarify its content, may I refer to Hansard for June 4, 1970, where as reported at page 7744 I moved an amendment to the bill which would have substituted for section 4 of the fishing zones act the following:
The fishing zones of Canada comprise all waters adjacent to the coasts of Canada, the natural resources of whose subjacent submarine areas Her Majesty in right of Canada has the right to dispose of or exploit, and such other areas of the sea adjacent to the coasts of Canada as may be prescribed by the governor in council pursuant to subsection (1) of section 5A.
The somewhat elaborate wording of my motion at that time was based on my desire that there should not be any deficiency in the form of my amendment. I used words which were parallel to those drafted for the use of the government bill on the Arctic waters pollution prevention measure which we had considered at about the same time. The response by the government to my amendment was made by the then Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, Mr. Jean-Pierre Goyer. In beginning his remarks he said, as recorded at page 7749 of Hansard for June 4, 1970:
Mr. Speaker, the proposed amendment to the bill to amend the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act would in effect extend the fishing zones of Canada to the outer limit of the continental margins adjacent to our coasts.
This pointed out, of course, that my proposal was identical in principle to the one that is now before us. I should like to add a few words to the statement made by the parliamentary secretary at that time. In closing his statement he said:
-the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni is premature and incompatible with the imperatives of the present situation.
Unfortunately, so far as I have been able to ascertain the position of the government on this subject has not really altered since that time. Therefore, I am perhaps a little concerned that the bill of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich may suffer the same fate as my amendment in that it will not receive the blessing of the majority of members who support the government.
I am, however, very encouraged that there is an inclination on the part of some members who sit on the same
April 21, 1972

side of the House as those who occupy the treasury benches to bring forward definitive proposals such as this, from time to time, for the consideration of the House. This is a practice that should be encouraged, because it tends to put real zest and verve into the discussions in this chamber when members put forward ideas which may not necessarily receive the immediate and full blessing of the government.
In his comments earlier, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich made reference to a statement he apparently read in Western Fisheries. If I correctly understood the reference he was making, it was based on a release I made on this subject. Let me point out to the hon. member, in view of what he said about my statement, that this release was based on a very careful reading of the text of a statement made by Dr. Needier, who is head of the Canadian delegation in preparatory meetings of the forthcoming Law of the Sea Conference. I do not know whether the hon. member has read that statement, but if he has he will recognize that as far as the statement made by the official spokesman for Canada is concerned it was very clear that in so far as Canada is concerned our position is that there will be no fishing for salmon outside the territorial seas.
That was a matter of very great concern to the salmon troll fishermen on the west coast of Canada. If that was to be the Canadian position, it meant that a very substantial area, including the one to which the hon. member referred, where the Soviet Union has agreed to refrain from fishing, would be out of bounds so far as Canadian salmon fishermen are concerned. I made my comments on the basis of that statement.
Since that time, as the hon. member has quite correctly pointed out, some statements have been made by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) which indicate there has been some modification or elaboration of the position stated by Dr. Needier. I will not say this is directly the result of the public position I took on the matter, but I am sure the hon. member would not quarrel with me were I to suggest that the position I tried to put forward then was one that expressed the feeling of west coast salmon fishermen. They could see a very large part of their fishing area going down the drain if Canada took the position in advance that there should be no high seas fishing for salmon bound for our coasts.
I tried to make it clear-and I think this is equally as applicable to the Atlantic as to the Pacific-that none of us in Canada wanted to see this mid-ocean or high seas fishing for salmon taking immature fish. We take the position which is stated in the hon. member's bill and motions I have moved in this House, that species of fish such as salmon which migrate into the oceans of the world to feed and grow are the property of the coastal states in which they spawn and in which the young are reared. This is a compatible position both on the Atlantic and on the Pacific, and if I understood rightly what the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan) was saying in respect of his concern, which I share, about the imminent prospect of depletion, if not the extinction of Atlantic salmon, this is a position with which he would agree.
Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act
There must be recognition of the need, under some circumstances, for us to harvest our fish beyond the 12-mile zone, particularly species such as salmon. This may have reference only to the west coast, Pacific troll salmon fishery, but the proposal that the waters above the continental shelf and the resources in them should be considered the property of Canada, subject to management and control of marine life and the preservation of the quality of those waters, is so apparent and necessary that I think the Canadian government is foolish in hesitating to state it as the declared position of this country.
The fact that we have, apparently without opposition, a right to the resources lying below these waters makes it an anachronism that what lies above the seabed is not equally our responsibility to conserve and harvest. There may be some circumstances, for historic or other reasons, in which we may have to agree to work out reciprocal arrangements for intermingling our fisheries with those of the United States. I think this is true certainly as between ourselves and the United States on the Pacific coast because of the way our fishing stocks intermingle along the north American continental shelf. With that sort of exception, we must recognize that unless we and other nations are prepared to accept responsibility and assume this jurisdiction, the long-term prospects for the preservation of the living resources of the sea are indeed bleak.
I think I have said all that time permits me to say during this debate. In closing I should like to emphasize that I am happy to support the bill introduced by the hon. member. I concur in his suggestion that it should receive passage and be sent to the appropriate committee for study.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to say a few words about this extremely interesting bill which the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Anderson) has introduced.
In my opinion, it might seem curious that a member from the national capital area should be interested in problems which have little to do with his own constituency. I should like to congratulate the hon. member for British Columbia who introduced this very valuable bill, the importance of which is recognized by all those who are concerned by this matter of fishing zones and by the Territorial Sea Act.
I also suggest, as the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan) stated, that it may not be practical, as proposed in the bill, to establish the continental shelf as a fishing zone. If, in theory, this is feasible, it is very difficult to put this proposal into practice by establishing this sort of fishing zone.
It is also important to remember-and this is the objection which was put forward-that we must take all necessary steps in order to achieve true Canadian independence. We must also remember, however, that we are living in the international community, and that we should never make any unilateral statements nor pass any unilateral legislation on this important matter.

Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act
And this is so true, Mr. Speaker, that for many years, the government's foreign policy has always rejected unilateral statements, in order not to raise a general outcry in other countries, because as I mentioned earlier, one must have consultations especially about such an important matter as the one before us. And this is why Canada has such a good reputation in foreign countries: we have never made, during the last 25 or 30 years, any unilateral statements.
Also, when we discussed this important matter in the House, last year or in 1970, I think, at the time when we passed the bill concerning fishing zone limits, we had had consultations with about 15 countries which we were sure would give us their approval-which, incidentally, reinforced our position. In fact, those countries had told us: Go ahead and pass legislation, then we will discuss the other details relating to this important matter, for we have wanted for a long time the continental shelf to constitute the real limit of fishing zones.
The essential thing, in my opinion, is control of the resources which lie between the continental shelf and the water above it. It is far more important for us to control those resources than to adopt the principle according to which we would consider the continental shelf as the limit. This is a very important matter. In fact, it is only following consultation that Canada recently entered into agreements with France and England. Denmark has also
been mentioned. I feel that at the Law of the Sea Conference in 1973, we will be able to reach conclusions which will allow us to discuss this important problem and find answers without offending the countries which come to fish in our waters.
Anybody who is a nationalist wishes Canada always to be able to make its own decisions. We wish it indeed. However, as I said, you cannot, in an international community, act unilaterally and pass legislation which normally would suit this country but which might cause prejudice to the countries which deal with Canada.
